utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, on I guess it was 20th, last Friday, we had directed the parties to present oral arguments on the issue of whether or not the statements of witnesses taken by the Defence may be produced for use by the Prosecutor on cross-examination of the witness once the witness testifies. At that time the Defence indicated they needed additional time. We have received the material submitted by the Defence yesterday and we have received the material submitted by the Prosecutor on Friday. Without suggesting what the burden might be with respect to this issue, Mr. Niemann, would you proceed first, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honour, I have prepared an outline of argument which may assist the Chamber while I go through this argument. I hand up a copy of that. There are four copies. The Defence have been provided with a copy of the outline, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sure your argument will be so orderly that we do not need it, but if you say it will help, we will look at it. We will not hold you, I suppose, to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the issue, it seems to us, for determination here is during the course of the trial and after the witness has testified in chief, can a cross-examining party call for the production of a previous relevant statement of the witness in possession of either the witness, the accused or the opposing party and does the Tribunal have the power to order the production of the relevant statement? Your Honours, I start with looking at Rule 54, a much quoted provision in the Rules, but in respect of this matter it is, in fact, quite specific. It provides, your Honours, that at the request of either party (and I am paraphrasing here) the Trial Chamber may issue such orders as may be necessary for the conduct of the trial. It goes on to refer to other matters, including subpoenas. Your Honours, in our submission, this provision, certainly in terms of giving the Chamber power, is very broad and would cover the situation with respect to the question in issue in this motion. In addition to that, your Honours, there is also Rule 98 which is additional to Rule 54, in our submission, and it provides that a Trial Chamber may order either party to produce additional evidence, and it may itself summons witnesses and order their attendance. In our submission, the reference to the word "evidence" in Rule 98 is wide enough to include matters which may be prior witness statements and which may be used to impeach the witness. So, it is our submission that there are at least two provisions available to the Chamber when it looks to what power it has to make the order that is requested by the Prosecution in this case. In determining the approach to be taken by the Chamber in resolution of any issue, it is our submission that, as a matter of general principle, the approach that the Chamber should take is one which favours the best fair determination of the matter consonant with the spirit of the Statute and general principles of law. Your Honours, this principle is reflected at least in one place in the Rules. It seems to us that it would not need to be so reflected as it is a general principle and should apply in any event, but one can see it reflected in Rule 89(B) where it says and it provides, "In cases not otherwise provided for in this Section, a Chamber shall apply rules of evidence which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before it and are consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law". We would, your Honours, urge you to approach this issue in a similar fashion with respect to this issue. Your Honours, the Rules themselves do not, in our submission, support the proposition that witness statements obtained by an accused or his or her counsel or on their behalf by third parties are for all purposes and at all times protected from production, whether it be on the basis of lawyer-client privilege or otherwise. In our submission, on the contrary, the Rules support the proposition that once it is determined that the evidence will be used at trial, then any restriction that may otherwise apply will be waived. Dealing with the question of pretrial discovery, we see in Rule 67(C) a reference to the Defence being required to make available to the Prosecutor for the Prosecutor's inspection "any books, documents, photographs and tangible objects which are within the custody and control of the Defence and which it intends to use as evidence at the trial". In our submission, the words "intends to use as evidence at the trial" is the factor for consideration here. If there is to be a principle of legal professional privilege applicable as such, then that may well apply up until the time when a decision is made to use the material at trial. It may be said, well, of course, this provision is not triggered unless a similar request is made by the Defence under Rule 66(B) of the Rules, and that is a Rule which provides a general inspection by the Defence of material in possession of the Prosecution. In our submission, your Honours, Rule 66(B) trigger, if I can call it that, has nothing to do with the issue of legal professional privilege at all. It merely goes to the question, if such a request for an inspection is made by the Defence upon the Prosecution, then an equal right of inspection is available to the Prosecution of Defence material. So the point I wish to make by this is that if there was a right of inspection by the Prosecution, the limitation upon the Prosecutor's right of inspection is the limitation imposed by the reference to the intention to use it at trial. So once that intention is made, it is our submission that any privileges that might otherwise attach are not contemplated to obstruct the application of this provision to the right of the Prosecutor to inspect. It may be that the Defence could still raise some objection based on privilege and that matter could be litigated as such, but it is not contemplated that that will happen because, in our submission, there is an assumption that once you either determine that you are going to use the matter at trial or, alternatively, you elect to call the witness and, therefore, present the evidence at the trial, there is, in effect, a waiver of any privileges that might otherwise have attached. Your Honours, Rule 70(A) is a provision in the Rules which deals with what is commonly known as work-product. It provides that, "Notwithstanding the provisions of Rules 66 and 67", so at the outset it does make itself exceptional to 66 and 67, in other words, 66 and 67 do not apply to "reports, memoranda, or other internal documents prepared by a party, its assistants or representatives in connection with the investigation or preparation of the case, are not subject to disclosure". In our submission, your Honours, this provision goes to what is referred to as "internal documents", so where it says, "reports, memoranda, or other internal documents", it is all reports and memoranda which are internal to the party. That is why I say that there may be a privilege that operates up until the time that you elect to either call the witness or you make a decision that we are going to rely on this material for the purposes of trial. It then ceases to be internal. The word "internal", in my submission, relates to the situation prior to the decision is made or prior to the calling of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But, I gather, Mr. Niemann -- excuse me, if I may ask you just one question -- according to your position, Rule 70(A) would not include a privilege on the part of the Defence to withhold witness statements once the witness testifies?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does it include or does it protect the right, that is 70(A), to withhold witness statements at the discovery stage, pretrial?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, it does not if a determination is made at that stage that the witness statement or the evidence will be used at trial because, in my submission, that is the effect of Rule 67(C).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 67(C) is the reciprocal discovery provision. In other words, if the Defence asks for material under 66(B), then that triggers 67(C) which would require it to provide reciprocal discovery. But you are saying that Rule 70(A) which talks about the protection of internal memoranda etc., does not act as a privilege against disclosure of statements by either party, because Rule 70(A) says, "Notwithstanding the provisions of Rule 66" which governs the Prosecution's right to provide discovery ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- or obligation to provide discovery to the Defence. So it says, "Notwithstanding Rule 66 and notwithstanding Rule 67", and 67(C) is the obligation on the part of the Defence to provide reciprocal discovery, it then goes on to say that notwithstanding the obligations under these Rules, you are not required to provide internal memoranda, etc."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are saying then that 70(A) excludes statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, in this very limited circumstance. It would at least in certain ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because it would violate 66(A) because in 66(A) the Prosecutor has to give statements, and then in 70(A) it says, notwithstanding 66 and 67, you do not have to give internal memoranda. So, if it relates to statements, what does 70(A) do to 66(A)? It knocks it right out?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. It may be that the wording of 66(A) is broader, but 66(A) deals with material that the Prosecutor relied upon in order to found the indictment. There is an assumption on that basis. I am trying ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It includes the obligation to provide statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And you cannot rely on Rule 70(A) by saying that it is privileged?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We can in circumstances where it is not intended to use the material as evidence in the proceedings. It is the intention to use it as evidence, in our submission ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then it is no longer protected from pretrial discovery?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. It may be, your Honours, that Rule 70(A) could be interpreted wider than the way I have by reference to memoranda or other internal documents does not include statements itself. I mean, that is another interpretation. I was specifically dealing with it in terms of, if there is a privilege that attaches to statements by the Defence, that those documents lose that privilege in the event of an intention to call the witness to give evidence or, alternatively, to decide to use that evidence in the proceedings. It may be, your Honours, that one could interpret Rule 70 as being much narrower and excluding statements as such.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You recognise then, though, that the Defence has no obligation to provide witness statements to the Prosecution pretrial, unless the reciprocal discovery provisions in 67(C) become applicable, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may be in terms of rights, the Prosecution has no rights, unless it triggers the Rule 66(C). That does not prevent the Prosecution from submitting that statements of witnesses that are intended to be used during the course of the proceedings by the Defence should, for the efficient conduct of the proceedings and the Chamber, be made available. That is another matter. The right as such would seem to be triggered by an application by the Defence under Rule 66(B) and that would then flow to Rule 67(C). That is why I say that under Rule 67(C) statements are available. If there is any limitation or any ability by the Defence to prevent the Prosecution from having those statements, it would be based on an argument that they are internal and it is not intended to use them for the purposes of evidence in the proceedings. There is a variation in jurisdictions on this matter, but there seems to be very solid law in some jurisdictions which say the Defence should be free to go and obtain statements from a wide range of people, and then at a subsequent stage elect which of those statements or which of those witnesses they intend to call as part of their Defence. It only becomes available, in our submission, for inspection once that election is made, unless of course there is some other overriding principle, such as malafides or something which I am not addressing here. I am just talking about the decision of the attorney for the accused going out and exploring all the possibilities in order for him or her to determine what sort of defence to provide.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So the obligation then on the part of the Defence to provide witness statements of its witnesses, pretrial then, is founded in Rule 67(C) ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- which would require then that reciprocal discovery provision come into being, that is, that the Defence have asked for discovery under 66(B), and there would be no privilege at that time protecting the Defence from giving statements, if it invoked the reciprocal discovery provision ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- unless you were to interpret Rule 70(A) as protecting witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, in my submission, there is no basis to interpret that because of the word "internal" that appears there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But we are beyond that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are beyond pretrial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I refer to this merely to illustrate that a general proposition that statements taken by an accused or his counsel of witnesses have this sort of general blanket protection which prevents them from ever being disclosed. Your Honours, in our submission the full ambit of legal provisional privilege, or lawyer-client privilege, is contained in both Rule 70(A) and Rule 97 of the Rules. Rule 97 specifically deals with lawyer-client privilege. It provides: "All communications between lawyer and client", and only lawyer and client, "shall be regarded as privileged, and consequently not subject to disclosure at trial, unless the client consents to such disclosure; or", interestingly, "the client has voluntarily disclosed the content of the communication to a third party, and that party then gives evidence of that disclosure". I am not calling that in aid to say that it specifically applies here, but the principle applies here. The principle is that if you have a right to privilege, then that right can be waived and one of the ways in which it is waived can be the person giving evidence. In my submission, that is what happens when a Defence witness comes before the Chamber and gives evidence, then if any privilege did attach up until that time, the moment they give evidence in the witness box, then any privilege that may have attached to a statement that that witness gave in the preparatory stage of the Defence case is waived. It is our submission, your Honours, that when it comes to determining what is the ambit of lawyer-client privilege, legal professional privilege, one should look to these specific Rules of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal in order to make a determination of what applies. There is reference, your Honours, to the Defence to the right to silence. I will expand that more later in my submissions, but it is our submission that the right to silence is exclusive to the accused and it does not apply to circumstances where a witness is a third party testifying before the Chamber. Your Honours, under international law and, in particular, in reference to the UN Convention on Civil and Political Rights, the principle of a fair trial is the dominant principle. It is, and I am quoting, referring here, your Honours, to the CCPR, the Civil and Political Rights Commentary on that Covenant which we will make available to your Honours. I do not have a copy of it just at the moment -- yes, it has been made available to your Honours. I am sorry. The reference I am referring to, your Honours, is at page 246 of the Commentary which your Honours have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Is this the work by Harris O'Boyle and Warbrick?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. It is an N.P. Engel, Publisher, Kehl, Strasbourg. It is a document that should look like that. It was just provided to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Page 246, your Honour, paragraph 19. Your Honours, paragraph 19 refers to Article 14(1). Your Honours may recall that Article 14(1) is in terms similar to the provisions in our Statute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is 21(A).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 21, yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (A), I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It contains similar guarantees. It is not word for word the same, but it is in general similar. In paragraph 19 there the learned author says: "This principle is at the centre of the civil and criminal procedural guarantee and, with respect to criminal jurisdiction, is specified by a number of concrete rights in Articles 14 and 15. The right to a fair trial is, however, broader than the sum of these individual rights." Then it goes on in paragraph 20: "The most important criterion of a fair trial is the principle of 'equality of arms' between the plaintiff and respondent or the prosecutor and defendant". Further on down in the same paragraph, five lines down, the next sentence: "In addition, procedural rights, such as inspection of records or submission of evidence, must be dealt with in a manner equal for both parties". Your Honours, in our submission, when dealing with this question as a general principle, there is absolutely no doubt that if the Prosecution called a witness and had a statement that that witness had given to the Prosecution at an earlier stage and the Prosecution had not disclosed it -- it has an obligation to disclose it, but I am premising this on the basis that it had not disclosed it -- your Honours would feel, I am sure, constrained to order the Prosecution to make that available to the Defence to permit cross-examination. In our submission, if that were the approach to be taken with the Prosecution witness, then in dealing with the principles of international law and the equality of arms, and bearing in mind that the reference here to equality of arms is the equality between the Prosecutor and the defendant, then what applies to the Prosecution with respect to inspection and access to information, when it comes to a general principle, should apply equally to the Prosecution as it applies to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But now these cases come from civil law systems and there is reference to a proceeding under Federal Bankruptcy Law. I think that the Defence has given us two cases or reference to cases that deal with that. In civil law system, of course, we would not be having this discussion because the investigating Judge or Magistrate -- I should ask Mr. Marro to help me out with the terminology -- but in any case that person would investigate and that person would gather all of the statements of witnesses for the Defence, witnesses for the Prosecution, the Prosecution gets a packet with all of the witnesses statements and other material and the Defence does too. So, clearly, there should be this equality of arms under the civil law system. Each side would have statements of witnesses of the other side. Our Rules try to incorporate both civil and common law notions, but at least, as they relate to pretrial discovery, it appears that they are more adversarial in nature and more akin to common law, and that until you get to the reciprocal obligation under 67(C) the Defence would not have that obligation to produce. So what I am saying is, yes, that principle does apply and in civil law systems everything would be on the table. But that is not where we are. So, how does that apply in our Rules, since we are not bound by national systems, how does that apply? How does that fit in our Rules?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Covenant reference that I am referring to is the United Nations Covenant so it is not limited to the European situation alone, although the foundation for it may be reference to civil law cases. But we would argue that the provision at civil law does not assist much in the determination of this question because of the very matter that your Honours have referred to. But, in terms of dealing with the question of these principles under international law, the principle of equality of arms is the most important criteria to be applied. In our submission, that makes no difference, whether it be a procedure under the Rules of this Tribunal or under civil law or generally because this is the approach that we would urge your Honours to take, having regard to the fact that this is an international jurisdiction. Whilst the specific Rules of the Tribunal may reflect an adversarial system, and in respect of those Rules, of course, all the parties are bound by the letter of those provisions, but we are dealing here, in our submission, with something that is not expressly stipulated. When it comes to a resolution of an issue which is not expressly stipulated, we would urge your Honours to have regard to the international law applicable in this area and the principle of international law which is said by the learned author of this commentary to be the dominant principle as that of equality of arms. So the point I was making was in the absence of any specific Rules, which there are no specific rules dealing with the very question that now confronts your Honours, we would argue that the approach to be adopted is the approach that would be applied in international law. Your Honours, going on in the little handout that has been given to your Honours, there is a reference in paragraph 52 in the middle of the paragraph when dealing with the calling and examining of witnesses in a similar vein. There is a reference there about 10 lines from the top: "The final version, adopted in 1952 on the basis of a British initiative by a vote" -- it refers to how it came into position -- "corresponds to the language of Article 6(3)", and then the important part that I refer your Honours to is this, it says: "As a result, the right of the accused to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf is subject to the restriction that this be 'under the same conditions as witnesses against him'. Criminal courts are thus provided with relatively broad discretion, but in summoning witnesses, they must not violate the principles of fairness and 'equality of arms'." Again it brings, if your Honours please, to this question of what is good for one party is good for another. Again, going over the page in the last sentence in paragraph 53 there is a reference there: "Of principal importance here is that the parties are treated equally with respect to the introduction of evidence by way of interrogation of witnesses". I make reference to these matters to reinforce the submission in our submission, that the approach that we would urge your Honours to take is what would you do to the Prosecution in the event of this issue arising? If you would say, "Well, the Prosecutor must produce the prior statement to permit cross-examination", then, in our submission, that is the approach that you should take with the Defence. I touched a moment ago, your Honours, on the question of self-incrimination because I believe it may also be an issue which is expanded upon by the Defence in their submissions. While I have this handout before your Honours, I will refer you to it. It is dealt with specifically on page 264, the final page there. In paragraph 59 the learned author states: "The prohibition of self-incrimination has its roots in English common law and today generally belongs to the essence of a fair trial, such that it must also be viewed as being covered by Article 6 of the European Convention. It relates only to the accused. Witnesses, on the other hand, may not refuse to testify". I immediately note that there is a provision specifically dealing with witnesses in our Rules. "The term 'to be compelled' refers to various forms of direct or indirect physical or psychological pressure, ranging from torture and inhuman treatment prohibited by Articles 7 and 10 to various methods of extortion or duress" and so forth. Your Honours ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is just because to be free from self-incrimination is a personal right that goes to the accused. The right to be free from self-incrimination is a personal right that goes to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and the point that we make, your Honours, is that it is limited to the accused. It is not something that can be expanded, as it were, in an umbrella fashion to everything that the Defence do on their side of the courtroom. So, in our submission, if a claim is raised that the accused does not have to produce these documents based on that principle, then we say, well, that does not apply to a witness who is called in the proceedings. Your Honours, the doctrine of legal, professional privilege has many features in common in the various jurisdictions and the various common law jurisdictions. There are some variations between the common law jurisdictions -- I am dealing specifically with them at the moment -- but, by and large, these variations are more cosmetic than substantive. For example, your Honours, in the United States there is a division between the work-product doctrine, lawyers' work-product doctrine, and the lawyer and client privilege. They seem to have been separated. This, in other jurisdictions, has tended to be wrapped up in the one doctrine. So, although the principles that apply are, essentially, the same, in the United States they have been divided, whereas in other jurisdictions, such as in the United Kingdom and in Australia, for example, they are rolled up into one principle.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is not the way I read Australian Evidence -- it is entitled "Adversary restrictions upon access to information". On 209 it says -- this is from Australia -- "It appears, therefore, that at common law the notion of legal professional-privilege embraces two privileges, a communications privilege, and a litigation privilege. It is important that these two privileges be kept distinct, for they each proceed from quite distinct and separate rationales, and I would suggest that much of the confusion that currently exists in this area is the consequence of not recognising that legal professional privilege embraces not one privilege but two. The difficulty in keeping the privileges distinct is compounded by the fact that they overlap where communications are made for the purpose of advice about litigation." Then there are several pages of discussion of the lawyer-client communications. That is on page 209. Then you get to page 216 where the author on Australian Evidence begins to discuss the second privilege which he calls "Material collected for litigation". He says: "This separate privilege is recognised in a number of recent Australian decisions. It exists to encourage the pursuit of adversary litigation, and is consequently unique to common law jurisdictions." Then on the next page, 217, he says: "In consequence, the litigation privilege is quite narrow. It extends to communications brought into existence at the instigation of client or lawyer to pursue litigation (for example, statements taken from witnesses), and to any other work-product of the lawyer". So it appears to me and also in Cross & Tapper, at least the 8th edition that we received from the Defence -- I do not have it readily to hand -- it also says that there are two privileges; the first one, a lawyer-client and then the litigation privilege. So statements, at least if you rely on these three decisions, would fall in the second privilege, that is, materials collected for litigation, as opposed to the first privilege which is the lawyer-client privilege which is expressed in our Rule, Rule 97. It is right in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right. There is certainly the legal professional privilege, as it is understood in Australia and England. It encompasses both privileges. The point I was really making is that often it is sort of wrapped up and dealt with as one doctrine, but certainly there is no question that both privileges operate, but it is a question of how you treat it. The only point I was making was that my interpretation of the law of the United States was that it seemed to separate them much more succinctly than the law of England or Australia. That is the only point I am making, but I do not for one minute quarrel with what your Honour has said. There is no question that there are two issues and can be easily treated as two separate privileges. In fact, your Honours, in a case that I think has been provided to your Honours of Baker v. Campbell, which is a decision of the High Court of Australia, 153 Commonwealth Law Reports, page 52 -- regrettably, I only have a copy extracted from the Lexis -- at page 88 of that -- it has not been provided?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No. I would be very interested to see what Mr. Justice Murphy says.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We do have the decision, though, that Judge Stephen ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of Grant v. Downs?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- wrote about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have one copy here but, if your Honour pleases, while I go through it I will have it put on the overhead projector which might assist in your Honours looking at it. Then I will undertake to make a copy available to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Could you arrange for copies to be made? Perhaps, Miss Sutherland, could you arrange for copies to be made or passed to one of our law clerks, and copies could be made right now and then returned to us. Did you get a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: One for the Defence as well. Then we will all read it while we listen. Excuse me. Go ahead, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I might come back to Baker v. Campbell while it is being copied. I will deal with what is said by the Court in Grant v. Downs, which is the other Australian case that I referred to, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You had better be careful because Judge Stephen, that is his case. That is the problem when you refer to cases that we have written -- not me but Judge Stephen. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The situation, your Honours, with respect to the two principles that I would refer to in Grant v. Downs is, firstly, the reference to what are the relevant principles in examining legal professional privilege. On page 682 of the decision, at the top of the page, it says in the first paragraph: "What then are the relevant principles of law governing the privilege which attaches to communications and materials submitted by a client to his solicitor for the purpose of advice or for the purpose of use in existing or anticipated litigation, in particular when the materials have been called into existence to serve more than one purpose", which is not the position here. It then goes on. I am making reference to this to draw attention to the position of law in Australia which is also developed in the Baker and Campbell case. There is a reference then to Seabrook v. British Transport, their Honours Justices Stephen, Mason and Murphy go on to say "contained a comprehensive review of the decided cases, illustrating as it does by reference to earlier judgments, that the essential elements of this head of privilege (which embraces communications and investigations made by the client as well as communications and work undertaken by the legal adviser" -- just stopping there for a moment, your Honours, you can see from that the approach in Australia (and, I would submit, the same in England) is often to roll the two together and deal with it that way -- "whether for use in litigation or for advice have been differently expressed from time to time. The difference is not one of expression only because, as his Lordship observed, the course of decision tended to keep the privilege within narrow confines until 1913". There is a reference to a decision of the Court of Appeal. "Thereafter, certainly until more recently, the decisions gave greater emphasis to the claim for privilege". Then the next sentence is of use: "It has been accepted that documents brought into existence after an accident pursuant to a standing instruction previously given may be privileged". So this is, in my submission, the question of bringing into existence documents which may include statements, certainly as it seems to be treated by the law in Australia, could and probably do have privilege attached to them right up until a point when that privilege is waived. So if one is approaching it from that point ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But you are not suggesting that Grant v. Downs assists you at all? The whole point of Grant v. Downs was whether the document was brought into existence for the purpose of litigation or whether it was part of a routine accident investigation procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I acknowledge, your Honour, that the facts of that case are not helpful to the situation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is not a witness statement case. This was a report. It was prepared by an institution, mental institution, I believe, that was submitted to their lawyers. The issue was whether or not that report was brought into existence for the sole purpose of litigation. Judge Stephen says that is what it has to be, the sole purpose, and finds that there are other purposes. So this would be, it appears, protected by the first privilege, the privilege that exists between lawyer and client, because that was their client. That report went to the lawyer. So the question then is even whether it is privileged, but if they find it is privileged it is because it fits in the first category. Communications between lawyers and clients are pretty sacrosanct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and they are dealt with specifically under our Rules under a different heading.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They are under 97. Judge Stephen narrows it from the British rule saying -- I do not know, Judge Stephen is better to tell me what he intended -- he narrows it, and then he says, though, in explaining why, "... The existence of the privilege reflects to the extent to which it is accorded the paramountcy of this public interest over a mere general public interest, which requires that in the interest of a fair trial litigation should be conducted on the footing that all relevant documentary evidence is available". He says that we are restricted in Australia to the sole purpose of balancing that, that public interest. So I too do not see how it really relates to this issue, but it is another judgment for us to read which we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The specific facts of the case do not assist, but I would argue it assists in reaching understanding if one is to canvass the law of the various jurisdictions. It assists in some understanding of that law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But, I am sorry, it assists only in showing that legal professional privilege does apply to witness statements which are produced solely for the purpose of litigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, so that it goes directly against you to that extent, if you regard it as applicable at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It does but ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Unless there is waiver.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- unless there is waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And you say there is waiver when the witness gives evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. In our submission, that is the moment or, under our Rules, it in fact can occur earlier, that is, once a decision is made to use this evidence in the proceedings, then the waiver ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is certainly authority to that effect that I would be very interested to see.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was it a witness statement or does it sound like something that is in 70(A) of our Rules, that is, a report, memoranda, or other internal documents? It may not be critical to your position. I just wanted to understand your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because, as I understand it, it was the client who prepared this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In Grant v. Downs?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that right? Was it a client, Judge Stephens?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: My recollection of it is confined entirely to reading this almost illegible copy that I have. I certainly do not recall it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought it was a mental institution; it was a patient who escaped and was discovered, incurred bronchial pneumonia or something and the mental institution, a client, prepares a report and gives it to his lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not put it any higher, your Honours, than simply it may assist the Chamber to have an understanding of how the law has been interpreted in that jurisdiction. I am in the process of going through the various jurisdictions. Your Honours, one of the matters that I would submit is appropriate for consideration in this issue is this process of calling for documents and whether, as it is understood in the law of England, the United Kingdom and Australia, whether there is provision or a practice which permits the calling for documents in the course of the trial. In our submission, there are numerous references that one can go to in relation to this question. Again, in the extracts of the Australian Evidence book by Ligertwood in paragraph 5.35 at page 227, which I again trust your Honours have been given that page?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I suppose, I was going to ask you, you referred to the commentaries, Blackstone, Cross on Evidence, I do not know whether you were referring to the 7th or 8th edition, but we now have the 8th edition, thanks to the Defence, but in any case you referred to Blackstone, Cross and is it Ligertwood?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Ligertwood.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But you also give us the Evidence Act from the criminal law of South Australia, is it section 29?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Section 29.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Which says that, "A witness may be cross-examined as to previous statements made by him in writing, or reduced into writing, relative to the subject matter of the cause, without the writing being shown to him; but if it is intended to contradict the witness by the writing, his attention must, before such contradictory proof can be given, be called to those parts of the writing which are to be used for the purpose of so contradicting him: provided always, that the judge, at any time during the trial, may require the production of the writing for his inspection; and may thereupon make such use of it, for the purposes of the trial, as he thinks fit". That is from South Australia. Then you give us a case from Canada, Peruta, is it, which seems to have the same rule, section 10, if I am correct, of their rules, of the Canada Evidence Act, that says: "On any trial a witness may be cross-examined as to previous statements made by him in writing, or reduced to writing, relative to the subject matter of the case, without the writing being shown to him, but, if it is intended to contradict the witness by the writing, his attention must, before the contradictory proof can be given, be called to those parts of the writing that are to be used for the purpose of so contradicting him, and the judge, at any time during the trial, may require the production of the writing for his inspection, and thereupon make such use of it for the purposes of the trial as he thinks fit". Those rules of evidence seem very similar to me, if not identical. But we do not have any interpretation of those rules, at least I did not receive any, other than the Peruta case, which I do not see in your outline. Are you going to tell us how this Rule 10 operates?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. There is -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Perhaps before you do that, I might read the next paragraph of Peruta which does comment on the section? It says: "The section gives a right to cross-examine as to a previous statement in writing; it does not give him the right to obtain a written statement in possession of the adverse party". The South Australian section comes, as does the Canadian, from English earlier origins.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and the right, in our submission, relates to the question of a right as opposed to the ability to request the Court to so provide it, as opposed to a right of the party to have it. In our submission, it regularly happens that a party in the proceedings in dealing with this question calls for the document. The document may be objected to on the basis of a claim for privilege. Because there is an ability of the opposing party to claim privilege, that ability precludes it from being a right of the other party, because it then falls to be determined by the Court as to whether or not the claim is made out, or whether or not the document is to be made available. In our submission, when dealing with that question, the issue is whether the Chamber or whether in these cases in South Australia or in England, which has a similar provision, section 5 of the English Act, does the Court have the ability to order the production of the document, and clearly it does. It does so in order to determine the matter between the parties and it may call for the document and put it to whatever use it thinks is appropriate for the proceedings. Although there was quoted a Canadian case which appeared to have a contra view to it, it is our submission that at no stage does the Canadian case prevent the Court from ordering the production of the document. The procedure, in our submission, is that one calls for the document and the Defence, or the other party, may make it available. Again the calling for it does not of itself create a right to have it, but it can be made available. In some jurisdictions, there are consequences that flow from the calling for the document and it being made available, but they are not matters to which, in our submission, it is necessary for your Honours to be concerned with. At no stage have I asserted that in interpreting Section 29 of the South Australian Act or Section 5 of the English Act or, indeed, the Canadian provisions, do these provisions create a right in the other party.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is not like the rule in the United States ---

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- 26.2 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure and the Military Courts-Martial Rule which would allow for the production of the witness statements, even of the Defence, after they have testified. But Mr. Justice Proulx -- I may be mispronouncing the name, P-R-O-U-L-X -- says in his concurring opinion on page 19: "Finally, the trial judge, in the exercise of his discretion and in the superior interest of justice, can allow access to the statement, and even order its production which can then work in favour of the prosecution". Then he goes on on page 20 to say: "However, I cannot conceive that the power to compel the Crown to produce the statement of a witness is a narrow and isolated power. I conceive it to be but one facet of a wider power to order production that flows from the ability of the Court to control its process so as to manifestly ensure fundamental fairness and see that the adversarial process is consistent with the interests of justice. Such a power must include the power to order production of the statement of an accused." He says "accused" but, as I recall, the issue was really whether the Crown could obtain all of the witness statements of the Defence witnesses at the commencement of the Defence's case in chief. The trial Judge said, "Yes, you may have them". It was reversed, of course, saying, "No, you do not get them when the Defence begins to put on its evidence", because they are privileged and there is no reciprocal discovery. But, once the witness testifies, as I read it at least, you get into this question. But there certainly is no absolute right for you to get all of these statements. The Judge needs to look at them first, I gather, to see whether there is any inconsistency, excise anything that is a work-product and then, perhaps, give them to you. I do not know. Mr. Niemann, I have interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have discussed Blackstone -- this outline is helpful -- Cross and Ligertwood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I can ask you for a page reference to Cross because the edition of Cross that I have does not go as far as 1000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour. We have a very old edition here. I have not been able to get my hands on a more recent one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: We have. It is all right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have 8 but it belongs to the Defence. Maybe at the recess we can look at what we need to, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, so far you have quoted authorities from Canada, Australia and the United States. In the Indian subcontinent there are specific provisions in the Evidence Act relating to privilege. Have you researched the authorities there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In relation to privilege, no, your Honour, I confess I have not touched on that. What I have obtained is some material on the criminal procedure in Malaysia in relation to impeachment of witnesses. Indeed, the provision in Malaysia, Section 145, as I understand it, provides that a witness may be cross-examined as to previous statements made by him in writing, or reduced in writing, and relevant to matters in question in the suit or the proceeding in which he is cross-examined without the writing being shown to him or being proved. But if it is intended to contradict him by writing, his attention must, before the writing can be proved, be called to those parts of it which are to be used for the purpose of contradicting him. So, so far it follows almost word for word the English and Australian provisions to which I referred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Except -- may I interrupt you -- that I think that particular provision has to be read in the light of specific provisions relating to privilege, sections 126 to 130, which also appear in the Indian Evidence Act. I think there are lots of authorities on that. Unfortunately, I have not got any textbook on it. Perhaps we could get access to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I might come back to your Honour on that if I can get access to this material? Regrettably, our library facilities here are somewhat limited when it comes to doing broad researches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But would you not agree that the passage you have just read has nothing at all to do with compelling the production from the other side of prior witness statements? It has everything to do with the fact that if one has in one's possession a contradictory prior statement of a witness for the opposition, one can then use it and there are rules about the extent to which you have to produce it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and certainly, your Honour is absolutely right, the point that I make, though, is the proviso, the proviso which I was about to say is not specifically incorporated in the Malaysian law as I see it, but has been interpreted to apply in the Malaysian law by case law. But in the English and Australian provision to which I referred, it does provide precisely what your Honour says, but then goes on to say, "provided that ... " -- I should go to it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: "... that the judge may order the production of the statement and use it as he sees fit". That is what is in Australia, Canada and England.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But that is not ordering the production, compelling the production, from a party who has a prior statement of its witness; that is when the cross-examining party happens to have a prior statement which contradicts the witness's evidence and the Judge can compel the production of it. You are not suggesting that the Judge can just, at his own volition, waive the professional privilege that otherwise applies, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I am not suggesting that, but I do not read Rule 29 or Rule 5 to be so limited as to prevent the Judge from ordering the other party to produce the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Really? I see.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It depends upon how you read the Canada case. You say that once a witness testifies, then to the extent that he has a privilege it is waived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and to the extent that there may be privilege attached to it. The privilege works to protect the statement in circumstances where the Defence, in exploration of what course it may take in presenting its defence, may have freedom to explore all options, and then to elect what option it wishes to take in order to present its case at trial. Once it has made that election, then the issue of privilege no longer has work to do because the other issues which could create all sorts of variations in the process at trial are precluded from the Prosecution, at least, from the Prosecutor, seeing it. But once the Defence make that election and say, "Right, we are going down this particular route and we are calling this particular witness", then, in our submission, it is not a question of privilege applying to it. Cross-examination is at large. One can ask questions and the ability to attack the credibility of a witness, which is most often the basis upon which these statements are sought, is a legitimate and proper exercise in the process of cross-examination. I go back to say that it is in the fair determination of the matter before the Court that the exercise of the Court's power to call for production of the documents must be there. The Court can look at it and say, "In the fair determination of it, I will order that it be produced and be made available". It may be that the court says, "No, there is a legitimate claim of privilege here which may arise as a basis of work-product which is to be excised". So that is why it is not a right of the Prosecutor. It is merely an ability to call for it, but the Court has the power, certainly. I would go so far to say, your Honours, that in the fair determination or disposal of the matter it may be necessary to go contrary to the claim of privilege and to produce the document, if the Court so orders. There may be bases upon which the Court could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But, as I understand it, you have no basis at all at the moment for suggesting that there is a contradictory prior statement. All you are doing is saying, "Did you make a statement?" Answer: "Yes", and then call for its production. Is that not the veriest fishing expedition?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. It is based upon material that was made available to the Prosecution which has been tendered in the form of a letter. It is based on the answers to the questions ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A letter was tendered to your Honours from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Saying there was a prior statement, yes, but not saying it was in any way contradictory, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Does that mean that with each Defence witness you can in cross-examination, because he has given evidence, require the production of his earlier witness statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We can call for the production.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And you can ask the Bench --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: To order its production.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- to order its production?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That seems to me to be the veriest fishing expedition.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 15 minutes. When we return, though, we will hear from you to finish up and then we will begin with the Defence's response so that we can finish up by 1 o'clock, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Have you copies of Baker v. Campbell there now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it has been organised.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, before the break Judge Stephen directed a question to me in relation to whether or not this exercise would amount to a fishing expedition. In our submission, no, because it is specific to what the witness was testifying. The statement is a statement relevant to what the witness has said. It is not fishing to test the credibility of the witness or, indeed, maybe it goes the other way and confirms the testimony of the witness, but that is not fishing. It is directly relevant to the issue for determination. In our submission, if it were to be a statement in relation to something else, then clearly we would not be seeking its production and the Court, presumably, would not order its production.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What do you mean "something else"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I mean, if it was a statement in relation to some other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: About the weather?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Of course you would not, that is an irrelevant remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, but the point I am making, your Honour, is that often fishing expeditions concern themselves with irrelevancies. In our submission, this is not relevant. It is relevant because it is a means and mechanism by which the credibility of the witness can be tested.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Maybe what is suggested as a fishing expedition is that you are enquiring about what the witness testified to on a prior occasion without first establishing some inconsistency. Where we are with respect to Witness W is that a question was asked by Mr. Tieger as to what he -- I realise it was in closed and so I want to be careful -- had said in this statement. Then there was an objection -- I have the transcript -- that that question was privileged. So at the point when Mr. Tieger was getting into what was said in that statement there was an objection. Then we conferred and ruled and you never really got into the contents of that statement. So, you never really made a showing in the present posture that the statement was inconsistent. So, assuming that you have to make that showing, and the failure to make that showing would constitute a fishing expedition, we are where we are because of how we have proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just to answer your Honour on that matter, in our submission, either way it is not irrelevant and it is quite impossible, obviously, if the party is not in possession of the statement to make any showing as to what the contents of the documents would reveal. But, in our submission, it is not fishing because in either way it may well be relevant. It may be relevant because it confirms that on a previous occasion the witness said this, or it may be relevant because it shows that there is an inconsistency. So, in our submission, it is not fishing in that sense. Fishing is where there is absolutely no idea whether or not there is anything there at all. You simply cast the line in and hope to find something. That is not the case here. Your Honours, quickly I would wish to take you to a provision that has now been incorporated into the law of New South Wales. In relation to Section 36 of the New South Wales Evidence Act, I have provided a copy of that to your Honours, just the last piece of paper that I handed to your Honours. It deals with the principle in Walker v. Walker which is where that issue of Section 29 of the South Australian Act and section 5 of the English Act come into play. But, in particular, section 36 is very interesting because it provides, and it is set out on the second page there, if your Honours could go to that: "The Court may order a person who is present at the hearing of a proceeding; and is compellable to give evidence in the proceeding; to give evidence and to produce documents or things even if a subpoena or other process requiring the person to attend for that purpose has not been duly served on the person". So in my submission, your Honour, here is a much more clearly expressed provision which sets out much more clearly the power of the Court to make such an order and an order in the absence of subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But is not the scope of that section well illustrated by its title? "A person may be examined without subpoena or other process", and all the section does is to say that somebody who is compellable, and that, presumably, excludes a spouse ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that presumably ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- and happens to be present at the hearing, can be ordered to give evidence. But are you suggesting that this deals with privilege and affects the law as to privilege?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. What I am saying is that it is another provision which deals with the process of the Court having the capacity and power to order production. It specifically provides the production or produce documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, in the absence of a subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But, surely, it is dealing with -- there is no such adjective, I suppose -- subpoena-able documents. It has nothing to do with the whole question of privilege. It is saying the fact that you have not subpoenaed a document does not prevent the Court from ordering its production.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not arguing that it has anything to do with privilege, your Honour. There are two issues here, one is the power to order, the other is the question of dealing with privilege. They are two separate issues. The issue that I merely cite in this form is that it is yet another example of a power to order.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But, to follow Judge Stephen's line, only if it is not privileged. If the statement belongs to the witness, and if, for example, the witness has the statement, perhaps the lawyer interviewed the witness, took a statement in writing, signed and the witness had an attorney with him and the witness says: "I want that statement to keep with me". If that witness has the statement, assuming that he has the right to have that statement because it is his, then that is the kind of thing that you could produce from that witness. You are not following me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You do not have to, just move along. That is the beauty of law! That is OK. We can move along.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the position in the United States, in my submission, is the most developed position anywhere in any jurisdiction that I have been able to locate. I would certainly urge your Honours to apply the law of the United States because it is the most progressive and apply it having regard to international principles. In my submission, to apply any other principle other than the principle that has now gone through the whole process and reached the point where the law is in the United States would be to apply a law which has not developed that far. In my submission, I could take you to a number of authorities, including a remark by your Honour Justice Stephen in Grant v. Downs which talks about this whole process of fair trial, the process of open proceedings and so forth. It seems to me that the United States has grappled with it and has actually introduced specific rules to deal with it. Certainly, I would be urging your Honours to apply the most progressive and up-to-date provision that there is available in common law jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sitting here as the only United States Judge between two Judges from a common law background. The Defence might argue that it is not progressive, it is going backwards. But, in any case, 89(A) of our rules of evidence, our 10 rules of evidence, say that the Tribunal shall not be bound by national rules of evidence. So whether it is progressive, going forward or retrogressive, going backwards, I do not know whether just because the United States has a rule requiring the turning over of witness statements of the Defence after they have testified, I do not know whether we should adopt it or not because we say right in our Rules we are not to be bound by national rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But, consistent with the Rules, your Honour, the general provisions as set out in Rule 89(B) encourage your Honours to apply the rules of evidence which best favour a fair determination of the matter before it and are consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law. In my submission, when doing so, it is appropriate to look to perhaps the advanced and progressive provisions that are available, certainly in common law jurisdictions where this issue arises, particularly in addressing issues of privilege. The foundation authority, your Honours, for the amendment to the law of the United States, and the law of the United States was not always as progressive as what it is now, and it has gone through a process of evolution, the sort of evolution that may well happen in all the other common law jurisdictions, did come perhaps to a head in the Supreme Court decision of the United States v. Nobles. I did wish to make some reference to parts of this decision because I think it is very instructive in seeing how the United States came to this position and how, ultimately, this ended up as forming part of the rules themselves. This, your Honours, was a criminal prosecution in the federal jurisdiction. In the case, the Defence counsel sought to impeach the credibility of key Prosecution witnesses. Perhaps before I go any further, I should give the citation for this decision, although I think I have done so in my outline. It is 422, United States, at 225: "When the investigator was called as a witness, the District Court stated that a copy of the investigator's report, inspected and edited by the Court in camera so as to excise references to matters not relevant to such statements, would have to be submitted to the prosecution for inspection at the completion of the investigator's testimony. When Defence counsel said he did not intend to produce the report, the court ruled that the investigator could not testify about his interviews with the witnesses". The principal decision of the Court is delivered by his Honour Mr. Justice Powell. His Honour at page 227 of the opinion crystallizes the question for determination by the Court in the following words. He says: "The question presented here is whether in these circumstances a federal trial court may compel the Defence to reveal the relevant portions of an investigator's report for the prosecution's use in cross-examining him". His Honour then goes on to deal with the facts and circumstances of the case. He deals with the whole issue of the adversarial system and quotes with approval a decision of the Supreme Court of the United States in the United States v. Nixon. This appears, if your Honours please, on the handout judgment at page 21. It is the second to last paragraph on page 21 where his Honour cites a direct quote from Nixon and it is instructive, your Honours, because it says: "We have elected to employ an adversary system of justice in which the parties contest all issues before a court of law. The need to develop all relevant facts in the adversary system is both fundamental and comprehensive. The ends of criminal justice would be defeated if judgments were to be founded on a partial or speculative presentation of the facts. The very integrity of the judicial system and public confidence in the system depend on full disclosure of all the facts, within the framework of the rules of evidence. To ensure that justice is done, it is imperative to the function of the courts that compulsory process be available for the production of evidence needed either by the prosecution or by the Defence." In my submission, your Honours, this is a coming together of what is at the very position here. When one looks at the international standards that apply to interpretation, and when one appreciates that the approach to be taken is the equality of arms and, in speaking of the equality of arms, it is the equality between the Prosecution and the Defence respectively, in my submission, his Honour's reference to the United States v. Nixon at this point is most instructive.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The reference to Nixon is very instructive in terms of having all of the relevant facts, but Nobles itself, though, was based on a finding that there was a waiver of the privilege because the investigator used the report for testimonial purposes. Of course, then once he uses the investigator's report that contains the statements of two witnesses, then there would be this waiver. The concurring opinion, though, in Nobles, perhaps, is more instructive because the concurring opinion by Justice White distinguishes between the work-product doctrine and the lawyer-client privilege, finding that that report itself would not be privileged but protected by pretrial discovery, citing Hickman v. Taylor, particularly a concurring opinion by Justice Jackson who, curiously, was Prosecutor in the Nuremberg trials. It was Justice Jackson's approach in Hickman v. Taylor which Nobles, the concurring opinion bases its approach, that from my perspective is more enlightening. The principle is certainly there involving United States v. Nixon. I guess that was Nixon as in President Nixon, is that so? I do not know. I have not gone to the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I confess I am not familiar with it other than the quote that is here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But, anyway, the direct holding, though, finds a waiver because of the use of the report by the investigator for testimonial purposes and we do not have that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, moving on to the issue of the right to silence, though, which, as I say, I foreshadow would arise in the Defence presentation: At page 23 Mr. Justice Powell deals with that question there. At the second paragraph he makes reference to the fact: "The Court of Appeals concluded that the Fifth Amendment renders criminal discovery 'basically a one way street'." Then he says: "Like many generalizations in constitutional law, this one is too broad." Then the next paragraph: "The Fifth Amendment privilege against compulsory self-incrimination is an 'intimate and personal one' which protects 'a private inner sanctum of individual feeling and thought and proscribes state intrusion to extract self-condemnation". The point being made, in my submission, your Honours, again reinforces this question of it being individual to the accused in the instances of this case. There is also a further reference, which I will not take your Honours to, at the bottom of the page to that issue as well. There is then on page 25 of the handout -- I will not read it out -- a reference to the work- product doctrine. That is further developed, your Honours, on pages 27. His Honour says in the second paragraph on page 27 when dealing with the work-product doctrine: "At its core, the work-product doctrine shelters the mental processes of the attorney, providing a privileged area within which he can analyse and prepare his client's case. But the doctrine is an intensely practical one, grounded in the realities of litigation in our adversary system. One of those realities is that attorneys often must rely on the assistance of investigators and others". The point I wish to extract from that reference there, your Honours, is this question of the lawyer having the freedom when defending an accused to be able to explore all possibilities, and included among that is the obtaining of statements, and then to have the freedom to elect which particular statements they may choose to use in the course of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That comes from the concurring opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think it does. In any case ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course that then is reflected by the amendment to the Rules in Rule 26.2. I do not think it is necessary for me to specifically read the whole extract there as it is available to your Honours. I am sure your Honours are familiar with it. But it deals with this whole question. It certainly, in my submission, having regard to the limited canvassing of the law that there is available in all the jurisdictions, is the pinnacle of all provisions available if one looks at a fair determination of the issues between the parties. In our submission, your Honours, if your Honours are to interpret the Statute of the Tribunal, it is appropriate, having regard to the fundamental principles of international law when it comes to interpreting such matters, to apply a provision such as this or similar to this which would permit the best determination and resolution of the issues between the parties. Before I conclude, your Honours, as promised, I have looked at the laws of Malaysia Evidence Act of 1971 and, in particular -- I regret that I do not have a copy available to hand to your Honours at the moment, but I will provide this to you -- Section 129 provides that, "No one shall be compelled to disclose to the court any confidential communication which has taken place between him and his legal professional adviser unless he offers himself as a witness, in which case he may be compelled to disclose any such communications as may appear to the court necessary to be known in order to explain any evidence which he has given, but no others." In our submission, this deals with the issue of the accused waiving the right of privilege, and it would appear to be waived once the accused decides to enter the witness box and gives evidence. It is, in our submission, the similar situation to which happens here, that if any privilege did attach, the process of entering the witness box waives that privilege, and that the request for production of the prior statements of the witness relevant to the issues is an appropriate request by the Prosecution and, in our submission, it is entirely proper for the Court to order such production.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Could I ask you a question? Really, your submission is based very largely, perhaps entirely, on there being a waiver by the witness giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Is there any authority at all to that effect? I do not recall it in any of the text on evidence. They deal with waiver but not, as I recall it, from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is one authority I just quoted, your Honour, that is section 129 of the Malaysian provision which I just quoted then, speaks of "No one shall be compelled to disclose confidential communications etc. unless he offers himself as a witness".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to look at that carefully, but I am thinking really of the textbooks on evidence. When they do deal with waiver, they do not specify that giving evidence amounts to waiver, do they?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I am not sure that I have any matters specifically that may assist your Honour there, but ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I will certainly have a look, but I just wondered whether you had a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a quote in Grant v. Downs which may be of assistance in terms of the process by which one deals with this. It appears in the decision of Justices Stephen, Mason and Murphy at page 688 at the very bottom of page in the judgment where it provides: "It is well accepted that the court in allowing production and inspection of documents exercises a judicial discretion. In so doing it needs to scrutinize with care claims of privilege made on the ground now under consideration. It is for the party claiming privilege to show that the documents for which the claim is made are privileged. He may succeed in achieving this objective by pointing to the nature of the documents or by evidence describing the circumstances in which they were brought into existence. But it should not be thought that the privilege is necessarily or conclusively established by resort to any verbal formula or ritual. The court has power to examine the documents for itself, a power which has perhaps been exercised too sparingly in the past, springing possibly from a misplaced reluctance to go behind the formal claim of privilege. It should not be forgotten that in many instances the character of the documents the subject of the claim will illuminate the purpose for which they were brought into existence." That may be assistance, if your Honour pleases, when dealing with, for example, work-product privilege which may be part and parcel of an otherwise verbatim record of the witness's testimony or witness's statement. So, in a situation where a claim is made to privilege based on the fact that it contains work-product, which is clearly covered by, for example, the Rules of the Tribunal, it seems to me, if your Honour pleases, that this reference that I have just referred to suggests that that should not prevent the Court from looking at it if such a claim were to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is an excellently worded passage, certainly!

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No doubt.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That again deals with the first privilege, that is, the privilege between lawyer and client. Again that opinion, that judgment, dealt with a report prepared by a client given to his counsel. So the issue is under what circumstances may an individual waive the lawyer-client privilege.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Your position is a witness's statement does not fit within a lawyer-client privilege. It fits within a protection against discovery perhaps reflected in Rule 70(A) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence which deal with pretrial matters. The only Rule we have on privilege is Rule 97 in our Rules of Evidence and that is lawyer and client privilege. So there is really a difference as I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, but -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
