utterances.text: But I do not even see the Defence -- the Defence has not once cited Rule 97 in the papers that they filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But the point I would make, your Honour, is that if your Honours are looking for authority to support the proposition of waiver ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- then that is to be found in Rule 67(C) which talks about the decision being made -- it talks about where it is going to be used in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, in my submission, once that decision is made, that operates in a sense in the same way as a waiver operates. So, in my submission, ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Even that privilege can be waived?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Even that privilege can be waived. The whole process of waiver is further reinforced by Rule 97 in the reference to the fact of the person entering the witness box and giving evidence. Unless there are any other matters, your Honour? Your Honours, I just need to draw your attention to the fact that in my outline I have referred in paragraph 9 in a reference to Grant v. Downs to page 608. I am informed that, in fact, the correct reference is 686.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I think I would prefer to confer with my colleagues before addressing the issue. May I suggest that we adjourn at this moment and start at 2 o'clock instead of half past 3?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is why we recessed early. We indicated when we returned we would like to hear your argument. So I would like you to go ahead, please, with that. We really have time constraints. We may have enough time to hear you some more and the Prosecutor some more, but I would like you to begin, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have your submission and we have looked at your submission you filed yesterday as well as the materials. We appreciate those. Some of them were not in English, but we have reviewed carefully the materials, at least, that were in English. If there is anything that you submitted that is in Dutch, you may want to help us out a little bit. So I am letting you know in advance our limitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that, your Honour. Perhaps I should start by asking your permission that if it comes to the technical aspects of common law, I feel more confident if those aspects may be discussed by Mr. Kay, if necessary. I will try to deal with it, but anyhow it would be fair if I concentrate on the civil law aspects and deal with the common law aspects as they are on the table. As we have expressed in our brief, your Honours, we take the position that we are not under an obligation to provide the Prosecution with any statements, whether signed, unsigned or produced by mechanical means, given on a previous occasion by witnesses who testified for the Defence in front of the Tribunal. We also oppose the idea that the Prosecution may question witnesses as to the content of any discussions they may have had with the representatives of the Defence. As you may have seen in our brief, we have explained that the basis of our position emerges from the international recognised principle that the burden of proof in a criminal case rests with the Prosecution and that the Defence should not be compelled to give any evidence against himself. We have taken the position that giving evidence here should be understood in the broadest sense to relate not only to testimony in court, but also supplying information to assist the Prosecution in proving its case. We have pointed out in the brief that such a position is consistent with Article 14 of the International Covenant and is also part of the Statute in Article 21. In relation between a Defence lawyer and his client, the Defence lawyer, on the one hand, acts on the instruction of his client. He does not accept instructions from other parties in the case. But, on the other hand, though, when it comes to the execution of his instructions, a Defence lawyer is independent; only he decides how to proceed within the law. Within this system, the Defence lawyer is the legal continuation of his client. He is the voice, the pen and the brains of the client when it comes to representing him in legal matters. As far as the Defence lawyer and the client in this system are one and the same to the outside world, rights of the client may also be exercised by the Defence lawyer. The right of the client to remain silent, therefore, is the basis of the professional privilege of the Defence lawyer. As you have rightly pointed out, your Honour, from this principle two privileges emerge. One is the basis of the privilege as such, that is any communication between the Defence lawyer and his client, and the second one is the logical continuation of being one and the same with his client when the Defence lawyer acts on instructions of his client. That is the second one we are dealing with here. We are not relying on the first one. The first one, though, is the basis to understand why the second one emerged. From that point of view, we have been looking into other systems to understand how this operates. We have been focusing on four questions: Does the system maintain the right to remain silent or are there indications to the contrary? Does the system maintain the professional privilege, both aspects, or are there indications to the contrary? Does the privilege encompass communications with third parties such as witnesses or are there indications to the contrary? Does a Defence lawyer have to disclose as requested for by the Prosecution or are there indications to the contrary? We make a distinction when we are going to discuss these questions between the right to cross-examine on the basis of previous statements and the obligation to disclose. That is the basis of our argument. We are not disputing the right to cross-examine on the basis of previous statements, if you have them. We are arguing that you cannot compel the Defence to disclose such previous statements. What have we found? How do these principles operate in the jurisdictions of the world? As far as we could in the limited time we had during the weekend, we researched the law in common law systems and civil law systems, as well as the trends in other systems such as the Islamic legal system and the Communist system. The general trend in all jurisdictions is that the right to remain silent emerges from the principle that no one should be compelled to incriminate himself or to assist the Prosecution in proving its case. That is all over the world the basis of the criminal justice system. We have found no system where an accused is not entitled to be defended by a lawyer. We found in all systems that a Defence lawyer is one and the same as, I just described, with his client. All systems recognise the role of the Defence lawyer and the necessity to work on the instructions of the client and, therefore, to investigate matters under his privilege. The leading principle is that the Defence lawyer is entitled to the same right as the client, as if the client were in the position to do all that work by himself. That being so, it appears that the principle of non-self-incrimination is not only a matter as regards the client, but also affects the role of his Defence lawyer and then we are in the second understanding of the professional privilege. Defence lawyers generally do have a professional privilege of this second type all over the world. So the scope of our research was to investigate whether legal systems provide for instruments that could be seen as an infringement of that second professional privilege. The general trend is that in most systems the judicial bodies are authorised, be it in most cases under certain restrictions, for example in the civil law systems the involvement of the Dean of the Bar, to ignore the professional privilege in both senses of a Defence lawyer if he is a suspect or an accused himself, or when he is presumed to keep the corpora et instrumenta delicti. These are generally recognised as exceptions and no others have been found. As far as we are concerned with the duties to assist the Prosecution in proving its case, as claimed by the Prosecution, we may pass to you the following information. Statements of Defence witnesses made on behalf of an accused by the Defence lawyers or their representatives in furtherance of the Defence preparation, are privileged and not subject to disclosure. This principle can be found in all adversarial systems known to the Defence, except for the United States. It has already been discussed extensively, so there seems little left for me, that in England on the basis of Lord Denman's Act that for more than 100 years it has been accepted that the legal privilege of this second type is encompassed in British law, that is that also in statutory provisions such as, for example, the Police and Criminal Evidence Act, acknowledge that communications between a professional legal adviser and his client or any person representing his client or between such an adviser or his client or any such representative and any other person, hence "and any other person", made in connection with or in contemplation of legal proceedings and for the purpose of such proceedings are protected. This provision may raise some questions related to what must have been then the purpose of those documents drawn up by the Defence, making notes or making notes of what a third party such as a witness may have said. Are any communications written down or not, should they only be made for the sole purpose to be used in the trial or is the purpose of enabling litigation a dominant position here? As I understand English law, it seems to me that the dominant purpose here is the leading principle. Therefore, we maintain the position that under English law as long as it was our dominant purpose to interview witnesses and to make notes about what they said, that such work is protected under the second type of privilege. We have found no evidence in the textbooks nor in the case law that says other things about this. So far we have no reason to believe that in English law there is any basis to be found that a Defence lawyer may be compelled to disclose any communication with third parties, such as witnesses orally or being written down on a document, unless there is a statutory provision which, we will argue, is not the case here. I will come to that later. In Canada we have found nothing that indicates that under Canadian law a Defence lawyer may be compelled to disclose previous statements of witnesses who are called to give evidence in court. On the contrary, if we look to the Canadian Charter as it is explained in the exhibit Annex B that we have given to you, it is our understanding that although the debate on disclosure has been concentrating on the duties of the Crown to disclose, it did not concentrate on any duty of the Defence, that is there are no provisions allowing the Court to impose any obligation on the Defence to disclose such previous statements. As a matter of fact, the case law presented by the Prosecution simply and very clearly says that such an obligation cannot be imposed on the Defence. So we really do not see how the case of the Crown v. Peruta might support their case. It is our understanding that also in the Canadian system Lord Denman's Act is applicable and it is exercised in the same way as it is in England. Therefore, we believe that the material handed over to you by the Prosecution does not support the position. On the contrary, we would say.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Wladimiroff, with respect to the last case that you referred to, Peruta, as I questioned Mr. Niemann, as I understand it, and it is important for me to understand the posture of the case and how it arose, again as I understand it there was an effort on the part of the prosecutor, the Crown, to request from the Defence all witness statements of its witnesses when the Defence began to offer its evidence on its case in-chief. The prosecutor says: "We want those statements." The trial judge gives them the statements. Appeal reverses, saying that there is a privilege to those statements, that in Canada there is no reciprocal discovery. Maybe that is what you are suggesting exists, but it is not there yet. There is no reciprocal discovery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Therefore, the Defence does not have to hand over those statements to you when they begin their case, but again as I read the opinion of Judge Proulx, when he discusses access to the statements that is when he says on page 19 that: "The trial Judge in the exercise of his discretion, and in the superior interests of justice, can allow access to the statement and even order its production which can work in favour of the prosecution." Then he goes on to say that: "I conceive it to be but one facet of a wider power to order production that flows from the ability of the Court to control its process so as manifestly ensure fundamental fairness and see that the adversarial process is consistent with the interests of justice. Such a power must include the power to order the production of the statement of an accused." What I am asking you to do then is to focus on, if you consider there is a difference, between pretrial discovery where at least this Court finds that there is no right in the Prosecutor because there does not exist reciprocal discovery, and then the right of the Judge to order the production of the statement and then allow the Prosecutor access to it for cross-examination. Is there a difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think, so your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because they recognise the privilege.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to us that a court can only order in trial the production of that kind of material if there is a statutory provision to that extent. If there is not the Judge cannot simply by his own discretion lift the professional privilege.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Again, let me ask you this. Where in our Rules does this privilege that you say protects the Defence from production of a witness statement, statement now, after the witness testifies? Where in our Rules does that privilege lie?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: To be frank with you, your Honour, that is the problem of the Rules of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is not there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There is so much not there, there is so much indeed not there, how many times have we not discussed the issue of we should not get technical? There are no technical rules here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So is there a rule in our Rules of procedure that would protect this production?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The Rules only respond to issues that have been discussed apparently between the Judges when drafting the Rules. The basis of your Rules, our Rules, is the Statute. The flavour of the Statute is that it recognises the principle that no one can be compelled to testify against himself or to incriminate himself or otherwise assist the Prosecution to prove its case. It is not expressis verbis in the Statute, but the flavour of it, notably if you compare it with the International Covenant and if you compare it with the comments on the International Covenant, makes it clear that the professional privilege is a part of our system in this Tribunal. Therefore, both privileges are involved here. There is no reason to presume that under the Statute the drafters of the Statute had only their thoughts focused on the first privilege and did not think about the second privilege. I cannot read in the minds of Judges, but apparently when the Judges drafted the Rules of disclosure they expressly confined themselves to the Rules as you did. The Defence is only obliged to disclose as far as special defences are involved, and then only to the extent to provide the other party with names, dates and places, not the statements as such. It is not under the Rules that we have any obligation at the pretrial stage to disclose any statement to the Prosecution, and you recognised that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you go on, in your submission on page -- I am not sure what page its, they are not numbered -- page 4, I think it is the fourth page, you say that Rule 70(A) protects all Defence materials. What I am trying to find out is where in our Rules is there a protection? I gather you say that Rule 70(A) protects all Defence material.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I would say that Rule 70 applies to both parties. It is the bottom line. It would not make sense to draft Rule 70 if there is no privilege.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So that is a privilege then that inures to the benefit of both the Prosecutor and the Defence not to produce certain materials?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, and the scope of that privilege is not identical.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand in terms of pretrial because of the different burdens, but that is a pretrial argument I think. Rule 67(C), however, does require reciprocal discovery and that is assuming that the Defence takes advantage of Rule 60(B) and requests additional material. Then the Defence is required to provide to the Prosecutor those materials that it intends to rely on at trial. Is it your position that 67(C) would protect the Defence from providing witness statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I take a different view, your Honour. I approach 67(C) from the assumption that if the Defence triggers 67(C), then apparently it waives its privilege.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. So then at least in our Rules if the reciprocal discovery mechanism kicks in, then, if you understand, applies?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then the Defence would be required to give its witness statements. So it seems to me that there are conditions under which witness statements can be waived, that is the privilege that, you say, attaches. That is just one example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Could I ask you in relation to that, do you regard a statement by a witness as a document which you would intend to use as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely not, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: In that case, 67(C) would not apply to witness statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely. We are going to argue that. We may waive our rights on the kind of material as listed here, but before I could address the observations of the Presiding Judge you put forward your question. We have no doubt that the statements we have written down as we appreciated what the witness might have said, is not a piece of evidence we are going to produce at any stage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If it is not a piece of evidence, then are we really talking about privileged matters or are we really talking about evidence that is outside of the arena of discovery? At least in a concurring opinion in the Nobles case written by Justice White, he makes that distinction and then he goes to back to Hickman v. Tailor. What he is saying is that some matters are really not evidence. There are really matters that just stay out of the pretrial discovery. So you now say it is not evidence. It seems to me I wonder what is the need for the privilege, or are we just saying that this is excluded from pretrial discovery?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The purpose of why we have done what we have done is to be able to understand what is the information that is floating around and to be able to decide who will be called. From that basis on the document, or whatever it is, serves as an instrument to examine the witness in court. It has no other purpose then.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So 70(A) then, as you indicated, protects all Defence materials, including statements, is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. That protection carries through, even though it is in part 5, I think, the pretrial part of our Rules, it carries through to the time of trial, is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could you say that again?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You say that Rule 70(A) gives the Defence a privilege not to produce statements of its witnesses, and I am asking you is that a privilege that carries on until the time of trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I do not see any reason why it should not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You see, we make a distinction between witnesses giving evidence in court and a witness statement which is for trial preparation and used during the trial to examine the witness by the moving party.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have 10 Rules of evidence and you have indicated there is a problem in that we do not have extensive Rules of Evidence, we do not have these technical rules like the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Intentionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But not for the purpose to ambush any of the parties.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Not for the purpose to ambush. We have been through this trial for I do not know how many weeks, and we have resolved questions like hearsay questions, leading questions, what is the scope of redirect, misleading questions. All of these issues we have resolved based on our 10 Rules of Evidence. What I suggest to you is that 89(B), I think it is 89(B), that says that the Judges may admit all evidence that is relevant and has probative value, is just designed just that way, to give the Judges latitude, that this is not a jury trial. Also these are trials before an International Tribunal that involve both civil and common law considerations. So we have 10 Rules of Evidence, but we have been ruling on these technical objections. As a matter of fact, we have one that we have to rule on that arose this morning. So if there was a Rule like the one in Canada, it is Rule 10, then would the Prosecutor be permitted to ask for the production of the Defence witness's statement and then have cross-examination of that witness after the witness testifies? If there was that specific Rule, if we chose to have that specific Rule in our Rules of Evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour. I may draw your attention to page 19 of that Canadian decision. It says: "Section 10 does not give the adverse party to the right to obtain the prior statement of a witness he wishes to cross-examine. Neither the spirit nor the text of this legislation can lead to another interpretation. However, within the limits of Section 10 a judge can authorise the production of the statement and, therefore, access to it. Other situations can occur during cross-examination. The situation, for example, where the witness would need to refresh his memory with the help of his prior statement, in which case both the party examining him and the adverse party would be allowed to examine the document. Finally, the trial judge in the exercise of his discretion and in the superior interests of justice, can allow access to the statement and even order its production which can then work in favour of the Prosecution."

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. That sentence and the one that I referred to on the next page it seems to me indicate that if there were a Section 10 we could order the production of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Only ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But there is not that rule. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We do not have a Rule ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But only if we use it, your Honour. Once again we make a distinction between what we use as evidence and what is in evidence and those materials we do not use.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But in this Quebec case they were not being used by the Defence. On the contrary, the Crown wanted to get them before the Defence even had an opportunity to put on its case. The trial judge gave them to the Defence. The Appeals Chamber said no, because there is no reciprocal discovery; there is this privilege. Nevertheless, at least the way that I read the case -- maybe we will read it differently -- is that notwithstanding this privilege, once the witness testifies then the Judge can order production and it may inure to the benefit of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We apparently read it differently. As we read it, as long as it is not in evidence and it will not be used as evidence it is privileged. Therefore, the judge cannot simply compel the Defence lawyer to produce it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is rare for a statement to come into evidence because it is implicitly hearsay under at least common law systems. So that a statement is not the kind of thing that you just offer into evidence. It is the kind of thing that is used for other purposes, like impeachment or to refresh a witness's recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But is not the presumption here that one of the parties is using the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought the Crown wanted to use it and tried to get it in advance of trial and the trial judge said no. But that is OK. We may read it differently. In any case, the privilege is found in Rule 70(A) and that privilege continues on to trial, as you see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. We do not see any reason why the roots of that principle should be dropped during trial, because it emerges from a principle that simply comes from the nemo tenetur principle, Latin for no one can be compelled to do anything that will harm his case or to testify himself or to assist the Prosecution. I do not see that that principle suddenly does not apply during trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess then until 2.35.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, would you like to continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I hope you will appreciate that I feel a little embarrassed to discuss matters of common law dealing with highly sophisticated and technical aspects related to that law. So I will try to deal with it as far as I can but, as I said at the very beginning, I would rather prefer my learned friend here to explain those technical details which I am not able to do as he can. So, I will go through the material, but if any question may arise, I would rather prefer him to address that, as far as common law is involved, if you agree with this approach.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, that is acceptable. We have your submission in terms of just presenting the argument. That is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. We were left with South Africa, as I see it, before going into Australia. As we see it, in South Africa law, all confidential oral or written communication made between the accused and his legal representative in the latter's professional capacity and which are made for the purpose of obtaining or giving legal advice are privileged and may not be disclosed in a Court of law, unless of course there is a waiver. Apparently, also in South African law, as you have seen on page 165 of the material we have handed over to you, statements obtained by the Defence from prospective Defence witnesses are also privileged in that system. As my learned friend can explain extensively to you, also in South Africa the same system operates as in England. It all derives from the same Act which has been in operation now for about 130 years. Listening to the Prosecution, it seems to us that their main argument is that during all these 130 years that Act has been misunderstood by the courts and practising lawyers. We believe that is not the right representation of the Act. We are referring to Lord Denman's Act. If I may proceed to Australia, it is a little bit risky what I am doing because I am arguing about an area of the law where we have a very learned experienced lawyer here who will try to explain to you, that also in Australian law there could have been a basis for the argument that the Prosecution may ask the court to compel Defence lawyers to hand over material such as previous statements. Our understanding of their law is that in Australia again the same system applies as in Great Britain -- it emerged from the same system -- and that is that, indeed, you have the right, you are permitted, to cross-examine a witness on his previous statements, but the law does not provide for an obligation for the other party, that is the Defence lawyer, to produce those statements. We have found no evidence in the material handed over by the Prosecution, nor in the case law, that a Defence lawyer may be compelled by the court to disclose such statements as long as these statements are not used as evidence in court by the Defence lawyer. That is, in our understanding, the leading principle here. So we feel that the material handed over by the Prosecution does not support their case. I may draw your attention to the annex B that we have produced where it deals with Australian Evidence by Ligertwood at page 222 when it says: "Therefore, the proof of a witness may be privileged, but if that witness is called to testify he or she cannot refuse to divulge his or her observations of the events in question. But this should be done without disclosing that this information is also contained in the privileged proof. This simple distinction between the communication or work-product and the information to which it may refer can be easily misunderstood". Indeed, I am afraid, the Prosecution did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, what page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: 222, your Honour. It starts with, "In the second place", and then it read as I did before. The case law ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are we to reserve questions regarding what you say to Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think that is what I am asking you. But Mr. Kay is quite willing to jump on his feet and to answer any of your questions, if you want to raise it now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I had a question about South Africa, I suppose I have a question about this, but you can go ahead. We have your submission. You can go through your submission and then I will ask questions. Is that acceptable to you? OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Looking to the Grant v. Downs case, it has already been discussed so there is little to add, I would say. I may note perhaps again that that case deals with civil case, not under the right to remain silent or the principles we have been discussing so far. So we feel that case is hardly relevant, but if relevant, it certainly does not support the position of the Prosecution -- on the contrary, I would say. The South Australian Evidence Act, the reference made by the Prosecution to section 29, again it does not say that by permission to use previous statements that permission also arises a possibility for the court to compel the Defence lawyer to produce such previous statement. It is not in this section. It is our understanding that it is also not South Australian law that the permission to use it in cross-examination arises an obligation to produce it, when such previous statement is under the privilege of the lawyer. We have explained to you that, indeed, it is under that second type of privilege. The reference made to the New South Wales provision, Concise Evidence Law by Blazey and others, at pages 30 and 31, as we understand it, those provisions that -- Judge Stephen already discussed that matter as far as Section 36 was involved -- does not refer to witness statements. But the other one, I mean Section 35, as we understand the Section, is absolutely not relevant to the case here at hand. We understand it to deal with the position where one of the parties uses a document but does not tender it. Then the other party may ask the Court to compel the proponent to tender it. That is quite a different position to what we are arguing here. So we also feel that the Prosecution may not rely on this Article or this Section to substantiate their case. I had little time to look into the Malaysia ones, so I think Mr. Kay will deal with that one. I will leave it where it is. I would rather prefer to proceed to civil law systems. Then I am more confident that I can tell you things I really know what I am talking about. There was an observation, your Honour, you made at the very beginning of this argument today that did surprise me because, if I remember that well, what you said was -- let me see, I have the reference here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If this were in a civil law system, we would not have this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Here it is. You said that each side will have the statements of the other side, everything will be on the table. I am afraid, your Honour, that that is not the case. Civil law systems, as you are well aware, work with investigating Judges to prepare a case. In that context, indeed, both parties will have access to all statements in the file of that investigating Judge. But, within that system, there is no provision that says that the Defence lawyer has access to the file of the Prosecution if that file contains material which is not in the file of the investigating Judge. The Prosecution has no access to the file of the defending lawyer if he has material that is not in the file of the investigating Judge. It has been written a lot about, could it be theoretically possible that the Prosecution has more in his file than the investigating Judge? If you try to consume all that theory about it, it simply comes down to the point that if the Prosecution is not presenting material in evidence at the moment the trial has started, it is irrelevant. So he should present it at the very beginning of the trial. He should give it to the investigating Judge or when the investigating Judge is handing over the file back to the Prosecution and the Prosecution decide, "Will I prosecute? Yes, I will", then by handing over the file to the Judge, it should be in. It cannot be case that there is anything in the file of the Prosecution he may relay only later on during the trial. Handing over the file to the Trial Chamber means that the Defence lawyer has still access to that file. If you look to the other side, the Defence lawyer may have spoken to potential witnesses. He may have made notes about it and may even have written down verbatim what those witnesses have said. They may even go that far that you take such a witness to a public notary to have an official record made up of what the witness has said. At no possible stage of the trial such material is evidence. Even when are produced such a statement written down by a public notary and that is the statement under oath, it will not be evidence. We can only produce evidence as it is listed in the law and the lawyer may not produce evidence himself. He simply cannot. So, working under the civil law systems means that you have a lot of material in your file which can never grow into evidence, whatever you do with it, unless -- unless -- you produce it in court and the Judge may find reason to call the witness and to hear him on that material, which material by itself is not the evidence but evidence is then given by the witness. So, even when you have a public notary who has written down a statement under oath of the witness, the Judge will call the witness because the paper itself is not evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So what happens to the statement now you produce it to the Judge and what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Then in our problem I would say you waive your right to keep it privileged, then the Judge may not use it as evidence because it is not listed in our law as evidence. In French law, as far as I am aware, it is the same, in Italian law it is the same, in German law it is the same too because you have this system of limited evidence. It is not free evidence. Not everything can be put in. It is a limited system. The issue we are ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask just on this question then, if I understand you correctly, the Defence does not have access to the Prosecution file?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Prosecution does not have access to the Defence file?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The investigating Judge or a Judge does the investigation, takes statements from witnesses, both for the Prosecution and for the Defence, puts them in a file and then each party has the statements of the other witnesses and only those may you use.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then, of course, if a witness testifies, then you may use that statement to cross-examine, I suppose? I do not know whether there is a rule, but at least you can do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In practice, it comes to that effect indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Even though it is a statement of a Defence witness, you may take that statement, cross-examine the witness and there is no specific rule allowing that, but that is the way it is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. So ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Take the case where the Defence counsel has a witness who for some reason has not been questioned by the investigating Judge, and in the course of the trial he wishes to introduce the evidence of that witness. Of course, he has a witness statement which he has taken from that witness. I assume that he can introduce that witness and have him give evidence, is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What you would do, under these circumstances, is the material you have in your file which you call a witness statement -- what is in a word? We would say, "These are my notes about what I know about that witness", but even if I went to a public notary and have it in a form you would call, indeed, a witness statement and we would call a witness statement, though not a piece of evidence but a witness statement, what I would do is ask the Judge permission to call for that witness. Then the Judge may direct the Prosecution to call for that witness, a witness on behalf of the Defence. It is very odd but you would ask the Prosecution ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You would ask the Prosecution to call him?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But the Prosecution will not know anything about what he might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: They are an officer of the court in that respect. The Court orders the Prosecution to call for a witness on behalf of the Defence. The Defence does not have the right in civil law systems to call for witnesses themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What does the unfortunate Prosecutor do suddenly confronted with someone he has never spoken to and knows nothing about what he can say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: He is only the instrument, your Honour. He calls for the witness. The witness will appear in the court and will be examined by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I see. All right. We have got to that stage and he is being examined by the Defence ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- and that has concluded. The next stage is, perhaps, that the prosecuting counsel can ask questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, to be more precise, in our system, the Judge starts questioning the witness and then the party who asked for that witness will question the witness after that and then, your example, the Prosecution will be the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: My critical question then is this: at any and if so what stage can either the Judge or the prosecuting counsel demand from the Defence his notes or his sworn statement of that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: None, never, because it is in our system irrelevant. I do make a distinction here. In your system, you make a distinction between material that has probative value related to the guilt or not and material that relates to, let us say, impeachment purposes, but may not be related to the guilt. That distinction is not in civil law systems. It may be indirectly an issue, but it is not regulated by the law. There is no case law about it, there is no statutory provision that deals with that distinction. None whatsoever. So what happens is that the question never arises that a Defence lawyer will be compelled to open his file. The only exception you will find in all jurisdictions over the Continent if that material is related to the guilt evidence in our sense, for example, when he is an accused himself or he is participating in any crime, if those materials were the corpora at instrumenta delicti, if they were part of the delicti itself or were instrumental for that crime. But, as far as he has prepared his case by talking to people, he cannot produce evidence by himself. He can only propose to the court to have a witness called and then the statement in court will be evidence, but what the lawyer prepares can never be evidence and can never be asked and is never asked. There is a wide understanding all over Europe that that material is not evidence, can never become evidence and is a part of your professional privilege.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What about the Prosecutor, his file, does the Defence have access to his file ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- to the extent that material -- so it is equal? Both sides, both the Defence and the Prosecutors stay out of each other's file? They are limited to what is in the investigating Judge's file?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There is a difference, though. If the Prosecution has material that is exculpatory for the Defence, he is under the obligation to produce it. If he has material that says it is (A) and the other one says it is A accent, he is free to choose which one he will use.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But any material that was not gathered by the investigating Judge, as opposed to, say, the Prosecutor who may go out and do his own investigation and talk with people, that is excluded from the Defence access, just as the Prosecutor cannot get at the Defence's file, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right, but the theory has it that at the end of the day when he hands over the file to the Court, he cannot have anything that has not been disclosed to the Defence. So if he has after all, it is excluded, it is inadmissible, because he should have disclosed it during the pretrial investigations.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So there the cards are truly on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, when you entered the trial, it should be on the desk on the part of the Prosecution. There is no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is this by rule -- are there rules -- or is the practice you have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is practice. Sometimes you see in systems like, for example, in Germany you have more specific rules because Germans do do things very properly, so you will have detailed rules about this. In the Netherlands, they are very vague, as they are in France. But the general practice is that at the very start of the trial the material should be there and disclosed to the Defence. The Defence is not under an obligation to disclose anything.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That tells me, I suppose, that a new practitioner would not have a whole lot of guidance about how to proceed in the civil law system, but I have been a lawyer too long to start over again. I think I will just stay here, but I understand. That does not violate, I gather, the accused's rights, does it, the fact that this kind of practice is a practice and not by rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You see, if you look at the literature, as I have done, for example, the Dutch one, you will read that this distinction which one could make between professional privilege in the context of the lawyer-client relationship should not be distinguished from the professional privilege as far as lawyers acting on behalf of his client. There are very good examples such as, for example, a doctor, if he wants to heal his client or patient, how you say that, it may be necessary to put questions to the family about diseases which are in the family or to put questions to a third party, for example, a partner of the patient with whom the patient had, for example, sexual relations. There might be a sexual disease involved. Then the doctor, to do his profession well, under the privilege of his profession, should be able to put forward questions to those third parties without the risk of disclosure. It is exactly the same as we feel it here in Europe with lawyers. You cannot do your job, prepare a case, if you are not able to communicate with third parties when those communications are not protected. We do not maintain, as is, apparently, the case in common law, that very sharp distinction between the material that may be used in terms of evidence related to the guilt and material that is related to impeachment purposes; you do not. You will see in court on the Continent that in most cases the Judge will not allow either party to go into areas which are not relevant for the guilt, solely for impeachment purposes. So you do not separate your material to these differences. It is all in one.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: President Cassesse, I believe -- maybe I should not attribute remarks to him -- at least in terms of our Rules, I suppose, has said -- I will be corrected if I am wrong and this certainly is not evidence -- that our Rules, although they combine both civil and common law systems, are tilted towards the common law system, and that is because in part our Statute is tilted towards the common law system. I could be wrong about what he said, but just from listening to you and looking at our Statute and our Rules, it looks that way except for 98 where we can produce evidence and, of course, on appeal the Appeals Chamber may call for new evidence which is not in our common law.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But, your Honour, your order -- 97, was it not? No, it is not. 98, it says: "A Trial Chamber may order either party to produce additional evidence", evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. So we have a lot of problems here, I would say, if we use words which may have a different meaning in different systems. That is one of the problems I am facing here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In common law, I do not think that a statement would be evidence except under certain circumstances, but anyway you are talking about civil law.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Those certain circumstances, your Honour, are giving rise to the problems we are discussing now. That is the problem we have. Anyhow, what I have done is presented to you an opinion of a Dutch law Professor dealing with the issue very clearly. He was asked in a case (in which one of my partners was involved) whether he had the privilege of non-disclosure on the basis of Article 218 of the Dutch Codes of Criminal Procedures as far as communications with third parties were involved. The answer on the last page is clearly, yes, you do have a privilege of non-disclosure related to your communication with third parties as long as you acted as lawyer on behalf of your client. In between, you will find, if you could read it, a lot about the reasoning of it. But just come down to the material I have handed over to you, that is the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure, you will find on page 219 an Article 106 which relates to that Article 218, as I have said. It simply says that everyone who is mentioned in Article 218 cannot be obliged or cannot be compelled to hand over any material which is under their privilege. It is very clear language and that is what I already told you. You cannot simply go to the Defence lawyer and say, "Well, we have the file of the investigating Judge, but we feel you might have more, give it". It is impossible. It is very clear in the law here. Article 218 in Dutch law does not list exactly who are under this privilege. It says that those who are obliged to keep secret all that has been entrusted to them or has become known to them in their professional capacity have the privilege of non-disclosure. It is for the judge to decide who is such a professional helper. It is established case law in evidence that Defence lawyers are. What you see in France and what you see in Italy is exactly the same system. You have a provision in the law dealing with those who are under that privilege. Then you will see that you cannot simply seize materials from them, nor can you order them to hand them over except for, and there you will have exceptions. It is exactly in the same system. Though I could not find all the details in France or in Italy that quick, I have produced all those parts I could find that indicate, indeed, that the system functions according to the same line of thinking. What I have done with the German one is -- that is more extensive. As I have already said, the Germans go more in detail and that is the reason why I gave it all. Their system is exactly the same, but the Germans make a distinction between material that has been entrusted to you and material that has become known to you, because that distinction acknowledged the distinction between the client-lawyer relation, then it has been entrusted to you, and the other relations of a lawyer acting on behalf of his client, then it has become known to the lawyer. In German case law though, they accept that also under specific circumstances in trial preparation also third parties may entrust you with material. So, it is more than just becoming known to you. That is the reason why I have given you this decision of the Trial Chamber of Frankfurt. That case dealt with an opinion of an expert witness which was given to the Defence lawyer. The Prosecution asked the Defence lawyer to hand over that opinion of the expert witness. The Court ruled that the Defence lawyer was not obliged to hand over that opinion to the Prosecution. Whatever the purpose of that opinion was, whatever in common law would be the argument, was that made for the full purpose to be evidence once or was it predominantly produced by the expert witness on request of the Defence lawyer to be used in evidence or was it not to be used in evidence but just to instruct the Defence lawyer, it is irrelevant in the continental system. So, the ruling was very clear on it. You cannot simply ask a Defence lawyer to produce material he has been given by third parties in order to prepare his case, whatever the preparation is, what the purpose of his preparation is. I must admit that the material I have given to you about Yugoslavia is quite extensive and I am not able to tell you all about it. The only thing I can tell you is that in Article 151 of the Codes of Criminal Procedure comes down to a stipulation that says: "No one can ask a witness or a citizen to produce evidence or to co-operate with an examination unless provided by law". It is my understanding, and it is in the textbook I have given you, that this expression of "no one is obliged to co-operate unless there is a statutory provision you have to". If you look into the statutory provisions, you will see under Article 226 of the Yugoslav Code of Criminal Procedure that the materials and the work-products of the Defence lawyer are protected. No one can compel him to disclose what is within his professional privilege. That is what it says. So that is all I can tell you about Yugoslavia. It seems to me, from what I have learned about it, that it is the same pattern again; no distinction between material to impeach or evidence. It is all the same. It is protected. You are not compelled to produce any evidence or any material. If I may proceed to the more global view from the European Court, I will do that by just passing along what I have done with the other systems, that is, the Islamic criminal justice systems. It is not very elaborate, but you will find in that material it simply shows there is no reason to believe that in those countries they take a different view. It seems to us, reading that Article, that also there they accept the principle of the right of the accused to remain silent. Therefore, as we understand it, there is no reason to believe that a lawyer acting under the same principle will have to disclose. As far as we are aware, there are no disclosure obligations whatsoever in that system. But I only can say these are indications we have got from that Article, that we have no positive information about that. That is all we can give you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Article indicated in the introduction that it was going to discuss the rights of the accused at ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Very promising.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- two stages, investigation and prosecution, and all that you gave us was investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And there it stops.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It stops at 107?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There is nothing else. We can give you the book, if you like. There is more interesting stuff indeed, but the author starts as very promising and then when the point would come ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He never addresses a word about the rights of the accused at trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So he needs to understand that when ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Again, your Honour, it is a taste of it. The taste of it is not that we have the feeling that in that system you have a different approach.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, not really because it just tells me about the investigation stage. I was very curious to find out what he had to say about the trial, but he ended it too soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is what he did. China, also nothing more than indications, are there any indications to believe that in Communist China the criminal justice systems takes a different view? Are there reasons to believe that the Defence lawyer is totally separated from his client, he may not have the same rights, he is under larger pressure, he may have to disclose. You cannot read anything about it directly, but if you sense a taste of what you read, it seems to us, for example, if you look into Article 80, the idea behind it seems to us that also in the context of a search you cannot compel a Defence lawyer to do anything that might assist the Prosecution to prove the guilt of his client, the defendant and certainly not to co-operate with the Prosecution for impeachment purposes. The same flavour you will find in Article 84. You will see there it comes down to the relevancy test. So we feel also here no positive indication. We cannot show you how it works, but there is no indication if you read their Code of Criminal Procedure that there is a different system there, that in those countries the lawyer has less rights than his own client and, therefore, this privilege is mutilated. No indication whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just one question on that, if you are going to respond to these questions, Article 36 says: "The testimony of witnesses must be subjected in the courtroom to the questioning and cross-examination of both sides, the Public Prosecutor and the victim and the defendant and the defender, and only after the testimony of witnesses on all sides has been heard and has undergone verification may it be used as a basis for determining a case". This is even more foreign to me than the Dutch system you described.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What does this verification mean? What kind of verification is there? Is the witness subject to being required to verify his testimony? Is it important that the Court have all evidence to make a credibility assessment or not? I do not know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question, but as we read it, it seems to us that also here you have an indication that the evidence must be presented in court and there is no such a system that either party can be compelled to put forward evidence that is not inside the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "Should the Tribunal ascertain that a witness has intentionally given false testimony or concealed criminal evidence, it shall handle" -- let me just finish the sentence -- "the matter according to law". Again I was wondering whether the Court were able to make a determination as to whether this witness has not been truthful or whether he has withheld evidence and what was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Not -- I would say as you may understand this line in the context of common law, that is, a separate issue has been raised now how to deal with that witness in court on the basis of impeachment. Impeachment, your Honour, as it seems to me, after reading all the material and thinking about it, is an issue that has been elaborated within the common law system.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So why are we looking at the civil law systems ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Because it teaches us ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- if the whole -- let me just finish -- if the issue as framed by the Prosecutor is whether a statement of a witness for the Defence may be used by the Prosecutor for cross-examination after the witness testifies. We are focusing on a pure impeachment issue, not on a pretrial production of witness statements. I understand from listening to you as much as I can the civil law system is that the investigating judge develops the case, gives it to the parties and that is the evidence. If the whole notions of impeachment really are not something that are considered in civil law, then maybe we need to go back to our common law authorities. I understand your position on those.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I would say there is more than that, your Honour. Although the impeachment has been elaborated in common law systems, how it works in common law systems is limited by the same principles as by which civil law systems and, apparently, other systems are ruled. That is the limit is set by the obligations of the parties. The Prosecution is under the obligation to prove its case and the defendant is not under the obligation to assist the Prosecution in that. That also relates to matters of impeachment. The issues may differ, impeachment of what, but the principles, apparently, are all over the world the same. You cannot separate a lawyer from his client. You cannot say that the privilege of a lawyer can be separated from that first understanding of the privilege by simply saying, "For impeachment purposes, we do not recognise your privilege. You are simply compelled to produce your evidence which you have in your file". You will see it nowhere except for the United States. That is what worries us because ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see it in Canada and ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see it in the opinion and we have a Canadian Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is not a ruling, your Honour. It is an opinion which was overruled by the others. It is not a ruling of the court. It is not held in Canada. So we feel that the issue, how far can the Court go in compelling the Defence to assist the Prosecution for impeachment purposes, is not a matter that can be dealt with by jurisprudence. It is a matter of statutory rules. If this Tribunal feels that that is appropriate (and we dispute that), all Judges should decide that and add it to the Rules. Then we have a very clear situation and everyone knows exactly where we stand. It is not to the discretion of the Trial Chamber to amend, effectively, the Rules to the extent we have been discussing today, because then Article 6 would ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, there is no question of having to amend Rules. The simple situation is the Rules do not deal with it. So that if one did order disclosure, it would not be a question of amending the Rules, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think it is, your Honour. After we have started a trial, there was no indication in the Rules whatsoever that at any stage of the trial, after we have started our case, after we have presented our first two witnesses ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge Stephen is trying to help you. What he is saying is it is not in the Rules, it is not a matter of changing the Rules. It is a matter of creating a new Rule, so take that help.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to confer with more words, so I am not going to address it again.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We do not have a Rule on hearsay. I know you really have been concerned about that. That is a subject of a decision that we entered as well as a concurrent separate opinion, basically saying, well, the decisions speak for themselves. We do not have a Rule on hearsay. We do not have a Rule on leading questions, as I said. We do not have a Rule on the scope of the evidence. We do not have a Rule on misleading evidence. Believe me, when the Rules were prepared, we received recommendations from countries and NGOs from all over the world. I am sure, if the United States had its way, the Rules would be much more specific, but they are not so specific intentionally. I think that comes through in our decision on hearsay. We have 10 Rules focusing on the admission of relevant and probative evidence, non-jury case, International Tribunal, civil and common law systems trying to come together to resolve questions involving international and humanitarian law. We have been through this trial and we have handled it. There is no Rule on how the Defence should proceed to use Prosecution statements for cross-examination, but we have allowed it. For example, there is no Rule that would say: You have to show the witness the statement first to see whether or not he adopts it and show the inconsistency to him, as is in Section 9, I guess, of the Canadian rule and whatever the rule is in Australia. We do not have a Rule like that. We have not required that you operate that way. We have used the discretion of the Trial Chamber in controlling evidentiary matters. It was done by design, but I understand your position. You wish there were more Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, no, your Honour. There are two issues here, perhaps three. We dealt with one, that is, how should we understand how these things operate in all jurisdictions? Now we come to another issue, how should it operate within this jurisdiction and this Tribunal? What we are saying here is that, reading the Rules, we are fully aware, for example, on hearsay evidence, that reading your Rule 89 it is not in there and there was some bottom line phrased in Rule 89. So we were aware of the problem. That is the reason why we raised it. That is ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except in your motion you were contending that the Rules do not allow for the admission of hearsay evidence. Our decision said that our Rules do not address that issue. Yes, they do not mention hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is not what I am saying. What I am saying is that we were fully aware by the text of Rule 89 of the hearsay problem. We may not like it and that is the reason why we have proposed our motion, but we were fully aware the Rules properly informed us about the problem. Dealing with disclosure, if you read the Rules about disclosure, they are drafted in a way, written in a way, that we read them as extensive. These are the Rules of disclosure within this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Not requiring you to give ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No warning whatsoever that during the trial we may be confronted with another understanding, a more extensive interpretation, no, not an extensive interpretation, adding to the Rules a new principle which is absolutely contradictory to what we feel is in the Rules, because the Rules show a closed system. The Prosecution is obliged to disclose because they have to support their indictment, and they have to provide in the Rules us with material. The Rules are very clear. We have no obligation to provide them with any material at the pretrial phase. As I said before, these Rules come from the same principle, who has the burden of the proof and what is the position of the Defence here? Apparently, you have chosen, the Judges have chosen, or the system, as has been described in the Rules, in the pretrial stage no obligation on the Defence, only to give limited information related to special defences. As I explained, after the trial has started, the principles are the same and you kept silent on that issue. So we understood that also the principle applies in trial and, therefore, no disclosure obligation whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask you just a few questions that really relate to the motion that was filed by the Prosecutor early on for Defence witnesses' statements? You may recall that the motion was filed because it was the position of the Prosecutor that there was an agreement between the Defence and the Prosecutor that each side would provide its witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It was not ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You disputed the existence of that agreement. Of course, the Prosecutor has offered as Exhibit 349 under seal a letter from the Defence listing its witnesses and indicating which ones you have a statement and for which ones you have a video. But, in any case, you have disputed that there was this agreement to exchange witness statements, but you sent a letter indicating for which witnesses you had a witness statement. The Prosecutor then filed a motion asking for all of the witness statements 30 days prior to the time that the Defence begins to offer its evidence. The Trial Chamber denied that motion saying that in the Prosecutor's motion they had failed to show any reasons which would entitle them to those witness statements, other than the need to have an "orderly trial", as I recall. So that was our decision at that time, but the motion that we were acting on at that time was a request for all of the statements 30 days before the witness testifies -- that sounds like what the Crown was asking for in the Peruta case -- and we denied that. We denied that. If you have indicated that there was no agreement, then at least that is a different position than the Prosecutor. But it is not really, this issue is not so much related to the Prosecutor. As I see it, it is more related to the Trial Chamber. We, Judges, will have to resolve credibility issues. That is what I like about Section 10 from Canada and a similar Section from Australia that allows the Judge to produce it. As a Judge, when I am called upon to resolve a credibility issue, what I have is testimony from Prosecution witnesses, use of prior statements by Defence counsel for impeachment purposes. It is very helpful to me in some instances to take a look at the witness and then listen to what else and try to resolve these very difficult credibility issues. But now, for the Defence witnesses, you have indicated that that should not be allowed because it is privileged ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, we should have known before.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- it is the privilege in 70(A) which, you say, carries on through trial. That is my problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We should have known before, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you had looked at the decision carefully you would have known before. Just because the Defence does not have to provide witness statements 30 days before they begin their case in chief, does not necessarily, it can be argued, mean that they are not relevant once a witness testifies for impeachment purposes in the interests of justice, in the interests of resolving credibility. But I understand, you say that you thought that was for all times, even though all they asked for was 30 days prior. They did not ask to use them for impeachment purposes. They said, "Give them to us 30 days before".

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not a matter of simply reading your decision and then the case is settled. It is the whole system as it is. The Statute, the Rules and your decision at no stage gave any indication that during trial, after we have started to present our witnesses, after we have selected our witnesses, after we have informed you about our witnesses, who will be called, that at the time of the third witness this problem will be raised and settled in the way as has been suspended now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber decides to overrule an objection that someone makes about the scope of redirect, do they say, "Well, look there is no rule. We had no idea that you were really going to tie us so tightly to this business of going beyond the scope of cross-examination. There is nothing in the Rules dealing with that. We had no idea that you were going to conduct these trials in such a technical way". I would say look at the 10 Rules. The 10 Rules guide us in trying to acquire the evidence that we consider is relevant and probative.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have tried to explain, your Honour, that dealing with the evidentiary rules we take a different position here. If you read those Rules, you will understand exactly what the problems are because you know they are not extensive. They are not exhaustive. It is a clear picture. We are dealing with ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But we have a rule on a lawyer-client privilege. It is in our Rules of Evidence. It says that communications between a client and a lawyer may not be disclosed at trial. It is right there. So if you interpreted that Rule to mean that they could not be used for impeachment, then that is the way that you read that Rule. Not a surprise, it is just your reading of the Rule. It is right in here and it is in the section on evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have been arguing that all communications between lawyer and client cannot be seen as a whole principle as such. It is one representation of the same principle. We do not understand Rule 97 in the context of the Statute, that the Rule curtails the principle as laid down in the Statute that professional privilege is more than only a lawyer client relation. As yourself explained to the Prosecution, it has two aspects. We believe that both aspects are in the Rules because it emerges from the Statute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought you said you did not have any indication from the Rules. Now you are saying that you have an indication, but the Rules were interpreting them wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have no indication in the Rules that there was any obligation to disclose beyond what has been extensively describe in the Rules.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. So the Rules are there. You interpret them a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, because the Rules should be understood in the context of the Statute. The Statute recognises, because it refers to the International Covenant, that there is a privilege and that a privilege is also including your contact with third parties. Indeed, we were confirmed in that belief because the Rules simply said that we are not to disclose anything with third parties. It says we have only to disclose to the Prosecution when we have a special defence and nothing more. Then you may say, "Well, that was not in our mind when we drafted these Rules", but that is very difficult for the lawyers, your Honour, to understand what has been in your minds when you wrote these Rules.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, no, I did not say it was in our mind. I say that we have a Rule on privilege. In the 10 Rules of evidence, we have a Rule on privilege. The question is whether or not that rule on privilege precludes the use by the Prosecutor of witness statements once the witness has testified. That is something that we can look at, but then you have said look to Rule 70(A). That precludes the disclosure or the use. So you have found two Rules in our evidence that you say support your position. I do not understand when you say that there is nothing in the Rules that deals with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am making a distinction, your Honour, between rules that show as not extensive and makes clear there is a lot left to the discretion of the Judges. That is, for example, the case when we talk about evidence. We also have Rules that show as exhaustive, they give you all, and then we learn in the trial that the Judges say, "Well, that is not what we meant, they are not exhaustive". That is our problem because we feel that the Rules on disclosure were exhaustive.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What I am suggesting to you is that if the existing Rules that we have, and you say in your submission that Rule 70(A) prohibits the disclosure, if we were to reach a different result, it is a question of our interpretation of that Rule. That is all. But I understand your position. I do not know what else we can say, but you can continue and say it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Indeed, it will come down to, will the Tribunal do it the American way by understanding internal documents, according to the federal rules -- that is what it all comes down to -- or do you interpret Rule 70(A) as seems to be the case in other common law jurisdictions and as seems to be the case in civil law jurisdictions? That is simply what we are arguing here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You want it to be interpreted to include statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. We want it to be interpreted as is the case in common law systems other than United States and the civil law system, that is, all material in the file of the defendant which is not produced as evidence is under the professional privilege.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. If it needs to be interpreted that way, I understand, then to incorporate the privilege, the second type privilege, the materials collected privilege.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Because one cannot separate it. A doctor cannot do his work ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
