utterances.text: If that is true, Rule 70 says: "Notwithstanding the provisions of Rules 66 and 67", and then it goes on to say, "internal documents" etc., "are not subject to disclosure or notification". OK?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. In Rule 66(A), the Prosecutor is required to give witness statements. So, how can 70(A) mean to say, notwithstanding what we said in 66, you do not have to give statements? That is preposterous.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Because, as I explained ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is not an American rule or a British rule or --

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Once again, your Honour, the scope might be different. The working of Rule 70, the scope of Rule 70(A) is not identical for both parties, because Rule 70(A) may not set aside a principle that is at stake in criminal cases, that is, the Prosecution will have to prove its case. So Rule 70(A) means, in the context of Defence lawyers, that our obligation does not go beyond 67(A)(ii), or if he waive by triggering 67(C) other material. 70(A) confirms that, indeed, what is in 67(A)(ii) is limited to a kind of information which is not confidential, is not privileged, cannot be privileged. It is simply passing names, places, times and that is it, not giving any statement whatsoever. That is confirmed in Rule 70(A). As far as the Prosecution is referring to Rule 70(A), 70(A) cannot set aside for the Prosecution that they have another obligation there, and that is to support their indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But then 67(C) is the reciprocal discovery. It says: "If the Defence makes a request pursuant to Sub-rule 66(B), the Prosecutor shall be entitled to inspect any books, documents photographs and tangible objects, which are within the custody or control of the defence and which it intends to use as evidence at trial". You say that that does not include statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, because we do not intend to use them as evidence at the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, it is supposed to make it reciprocal as it relates to 67(A). Under 67 -- 66(A), rather, the Prosecutor has to give statements but the reciprocity, as is reflected in 67, means that the Defence does not have to give statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, because (C) says very clearly "which it intends to use as evidence at the trial"; as we told you, we do not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It sounds to me as if the Rules are there. It is a question of interpreting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If it is privileged, you would say it cannot be used for impeachment purposes. If it is privileged, it is privileged and the Prosecutor nor the Court will have the right to produce it. We have the Rule that you say supports your privilege. It does not seem to me like it is an absence of Rules; it is a question of how we interpret our Rules, if we accept your position. If you say if it is privileged, it is privileged, we do not even get to impeachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, and on the basis of the Rules we thought that that privilege was respected because there were limited disclosure Rules and those disclosure Rules presented themselves as exhaustive. If I may, your Honour, let me try to proceed. We have gone lateral through the material. I think the material we have handed to you on the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights may speak for themselves. The Funka case is a leading case on the Continent. I may draw your attention to paragraph 41 of that case dealing with the merits of the complaint. The leading opinion you will find in paragraph 44. We have given you the whole decision so you will be able to see it in its own context. When it comes to the bottom line, again that you cannot compel someone to assist the prosecuting party.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The right not to assist the prosecuting party, is that founded in also Article 21 dealing with self-incrimination? That is the position that you took when the motion was filed pretrial for all of the witness statements, 30 days?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, 21(iv)(G), "... shall not be compelled to testify against himself or to confess guilt". That is what those decisions stand for?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: 21 is almost the same, substantially it is the same as Article 14 of the International Covenant. The leading opinion is that the Covenant is substantially the same as Article 6 of the European Convention, because Article 6, section 2, is understood by the European Court as appears from the Funka case in the same way.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You do not see a difference between the use of witness statements before -- or the Prosecutor acquiring them or having the right to obtain witness statements before a witness testifies and after the witness testifies in terms of the self-incrimination issue, you do not see a difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: From the principle, I do not see any difference whatsoever. The principle applies before the trial starts and when the trial is ongoing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Rule 26.2, I gather, the American rule, which stands out among all of them, which Mr. Niemann says is -- what did he say -- forward thinking or something, I do not know, progressive -- maybe it is retrogressive or whatever -- that rule provides that the witness statements shall be provided by the Defence after the witness testifies. In your judgment, does that violate the right to be free from self-incrimination, that rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, because it simply means that the lawyers are no longer working on the sole instruction on his own client; the client is not protected there when the Defence lawyer is not taking the necessary precautions to avoid such violations. Again, if you are aware of such a rule, then the statutory provisions in the United States do not compel a lawyer to break his professional secrecy because he can prepare the case in a different way to avoid that he will have material he will be compelled to produce. It is how the system works, how you should judge it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Nobles case, which considered this very issue, really has two parts to it. In the Nobles case in 1976, the Supreme Court held that it did not violate the right to be free from self-incrimination, that is, the use of this investigators's report. Thereafter, in 19 whenever it was, 77 or 78, was when rule 26.2 of the federal criminal procedure was enacted. So, what you had at that time was a decision by the United States Supreme Court finding no violation of self-incrimination before there was a rule in the rules of criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, but ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But the other issue dealing with waiver, I have already questioned Mr. Niemann about. I think that does not help us much because there the investigator actually made testimonial use of the report. But, as to the secondary holding in Nobles, that is a finding by the Supreme Court before 26.2 was enacted. So the lawyers did not have 26.2 to hold up and say, "Oh, this is what we can do".

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Might that not be explained, if I can? This is going far beyond what I should do, but I understand that the scope of the Fifth Amendment is not identical to what you will find in Article 6 of the European Convention. That has also, as I see it, much to do with the system of advocates under the European Convention and as the system operates in the United States. That is the reason why I started to explain that under the continental system or, at least, the system which is under the European Court of Human Rights, and I recognise the same in those common law systems that have derived from the English system, that the advocate, the barrister, or the advocate as it is on the Continent, has a different position. The profession functions not identical to the American lawyer. Therefore, it might be explained that the understanding of the Fifth Amendment in relation to how the Bar in the United States functions may have reasoned that decision. I really do not know, but that is my sense, because the instructions under which a barrister works are so different to what an American lawyer can do or should do or should not do. If I only refer, for example, to the Codes of Conduct, they differ so much. That might have reasons why within the limits of the Fifth Amendment they have decided. But whatever may be the reasons, I really cannot explain this to you. I only say that the international standard is that of the International Covenant. Yugoslavia is in Europe. There we have this European Convention. These two guidelines point to a quite different direction, whatever may have been the case in the United States.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I suppose we will have to check, in 1976 I would guess the right to be free from self-incrimination had been pretty well interpreted and probably more rights than exist now, because at that time you had Miranda and all of those rights. Now they have been going back. But in 1976, if I were to guess, it was at its higher point and it started coming down. But, at least in 1976, if we look at Nobles we probably can got some guidance, but I do not know. We are talking about ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But has there not always been a distinction between the lawyer and the client? I do remember, for example, all the discussions about paying your lawyer which raised a large problem in the United States if the source of that payment was in the context of crimes while, for example, on the Continent and in England we take a different view here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What, that you can do that or you cannot?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Under certain conditions, you can be paid indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In the United States you might lose it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Again we fear that the lawyer and the client are ultimately one; you cannot simply say, "No one is going to pay me, therefore, you will not have a lawyer". I may draw also your attention, your Honours, to the Niemietz case. There was a complaint about the search of his law office. He claimed that would give rise to a breach of Article 8 of the European Convention. I may draw your attention to paragraph 37 where the European Court held that the search impinged on professional secrecy to an extent that appears disproportionate in the circumstances. It has in this connection to be recalled that where a lawyer is involved, an encroachment on professional secrecy may have repercussions on the proper administration of justice and, hence, the risk guaranteed by Article 6 of the Convention. Again, you see, the link always back to Article 6 and the right not to incriminate yourself in the broadest sense also relating to the lawyer acting on behalf of his client.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What did they mean when they said "disproportionate in the circumstances"? Are there any circumstances where they can break into a lawyer's office?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, when the lawyer ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If there is not evidence of an ongoing crime, is there anything ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If the lawyer is involved in the crime himself or when those materials are the corpora et instrumenta of the crime itself.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So they were finding that that was not the case there and that is why it was disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It was not clear. The Prosecution has also referred to equality of arms which, I must say, was a very stunning argument. I have never read ever before that the Prosecution is arguing that they are entitled to the same treatment as the Defence is. I think this is a very close reading of what is really at stake here. As far as the Prosecution is referring to the phrase that the accused is entitled to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf, subject to the restriction that this be under the same conditions as witnesses against him, that phrase is so logical if you know about the civil law system, because you have to ask the Prosecution or the Court to call the witness. You cannot call the witnesses yourself. That is the problem. So, if the Prosecution has the right, according to the law, to call for witnesses and you, as the Defence lawyer, have not, you are dependent on a Court order or the co-operation of the Prosecution. Then the Convention says it would be highly unfair, at least in the context of a fair trial, if you were not able to call witnesses under the same conditions as witnesses against you. It makes sense in logic, if you understand the system. But it had nothing to do that if we are able to impeach Prosecution witnesses on material that has been handed over to us that the Prosecution may argue, well, then we have the right to compel the Defence to hand over material to us to impeach their witnesses, absolutely no basis in the Convention whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What was meant, before you leave that, on page 175 of the Law and Practice of the European Convention on Human Rights and the European Social Charter, where it said that the ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Help me again, your Honour, you were referring to -- I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: On page 175 it says: "The European Court of Human Rights stated the principle of equality of arms is only one feature of the wider concept of a fair trial which also includes the fundamental right that criminal proceedings should be adversarial. The right to an adversarial trial means in a criminal case that both Prosecution and Defence must be given opportunity to have knowledge of and comment on the observations filed and the evidence adduced by the other party". Then they were challenged. The French -- what system was that ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely clear to me because if you read the case law of the European Court on this, what you will see is that, for example, in Austria there were provisions in the law that excluded the defendant from access to certain parts of the file. In France, you will see the same. These cases have been brought to the European Court. They ruled, obviously, that you should have the same access to the file as the Prosecution. There are no cases, none whatsoever since 1950 when this all started, that ever the Prosecution complained that they had no access to the file of the defendant. That is outrageous. That would not be the case. The file is the file of the court. We have the system of a file. There is no file in common law systems. The file of the court is the file made by the investigating Judge or the file handed over by the Prosecution to the Court. Both parties should have the same access to that file and there is no file of the Defence lawyer involved here. It has nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The file is what has been collected, but it includes statements and both sides have access to it. In our adversarial common law system, we depend on the lawyers kind of to develop that, except that our Rules have a little taste of the civil law system in that they kind of put the Judge in there to elicit material, but you say it is illicit evidence and statements are not evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, as long as the Defence lawyer does not present that material as evidence. We do accept within the context of the common law a taste of the Rules of this Tribunal. For example, if we show to a witness a document and we do not tender it, we accept that the other party will say that the Court will have to rule that we will have to tender that, because by showing it to the witness in court we used it in court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But we do not have a Rule on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, but in the setting of what is happening here in this Court, we accepted that both parties, where there is no file, have to co-operate in finding what are the facts in this case. That is quite opposite to what the Prosecution is asking. They simply want access to our private file on material we are not going to use.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Have you completed your presentation? Mr. Kay has a number of questions and then, the Prosecution, do you have rebuttal? I think we had better stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Let me just see, your Honour. I think I have dealt with everything. Yes, I may refer your attention to the Brandstetter case. We have given the decision, so I think it is self-explanatory. That is all I had to say, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. Then, Mr. Kay, are you going to present then the common law aspects or do we just ask questions about common law?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, if I perhaps give a quick few minutes and then field the questions, that might be the best way?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may be seated. We are waiting for some of our staff. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, might I start, first of all, by reminding the Court that in the original motion by the Prosecution in April of this year that they referred in their argument that witnesses may be put on the stand to testify by the Defence and we would be withholding the statement from opposing counsel and the Court. It was very much in the mind of the Prosecution that these statements should be disclosed for impeachment purposes when they filed their motion earlier in the year. In the response filed by us, aware of that use of them, in paragraph G I stated that they would be primarily used as a device of impeachment. The Court may recollect that in oral argument I also referred to that matter. So, when the Court judgment was issued on 7th May, there was no matter in relation to the decision that indicated that statements would eventually be used at this stage of the trial potentially as an impeachment device. So, aware of the arguments, we embarked on the course of preparation of collecting our witnesses together with all the baggage of previous statements collected by lawyers not now on the team. We believed that the judgment we were given on 7th May gave us an absolute position in relation to that disclosure. It had been presented in this way by the Prosecution and denied by the Trial Chamber. We dealt with common law systems, but in the course of today the Malaysian Rules have been supplied to me. I know his Honour Judge Vohrah will be familiar with these. But in section 126 of the Evidence Act of 1950 of the laws of Malaysia -- I do not know whether that has been served on the Court just now -- it clearly states: "No advocate shall at any time be permitted, unless with his client's express consent, to disclose any communication made to him in the course and for the purpose of his employment as such advocate by or on behalf of his client, or to state the contents or condition of any document with which he has become acquainted in the course and for the purpose of his professional employment, or to disclose any advice given by him to his client in the course and for the purpose of such employment". Then there are the well-known exceptions which are apparent in every jurisdiction, that illegal purposes and crime or fraud will not be so protected. Illustrations are given within Section 126 and Section 128 is a section that deals with privilege not being waived by volunteering evidence: "If any party to a suit gives evidence therein at his own instance otherwise, he shall not be deemed to have consented thereby to such disclosure as is mentioned in Section 126; and if any party to a suit or proceeding calls any such advocate as a witness, he shall be deemed to have consented to the disclosure, only if he questions the advocate on matters which but for such question he would not be at liberty to disclose". Then Section 129 deals, in fact, with circumstances when confidential communications may be disclosed: "No one shall be compelled to disclose to the court any confidential communication which has taken place between him and his legal professional adviser unless he offers himself as a witness, in which case he may be compelled to disclose any such communications as may appear to the court to be necessary to be known in order", and here I underline "to explain any evidence which he has given, but no others". So this Statute, in our submission, envisages the concept of legal and client professional privilege, but there may be circumstances when an explanation is required by the Court when that be waived. The kind of circumstance that I am thinking of is if a defendant was to say, "My lawyer advised me not to answer any questions at the police station and that is why I gave no answer". In those circumstances, invoking section 129 of the laws of Malaysia, the Court would be entitled to an explanation as to whether that was the advice actually given by the lawyer. It is one that would require an explanation, but the overall umbrella section is that of Section 126. So the position here we say is identical in most, well, in all common law countries, bar the United States of America where they have specifically enacted through their parliament or legislature rules that otherwise vitiate the normal position within common law countries.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you one question then. It seems to me that we have agreed, based on the material that you have given me, that there are two privileges, a communications privilege and a litigation privilege. The litigation privilege is one that protects disclosure of confidential communications between lawyer and client. Then the other one, material collected for litigation which is referred to in the United States, perhaps, as the work-product doctrine, is the one that is unique to common law and it extends to products such as witness statements. This I get from the Australian Evidence discussion as well as Cross & Tapper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Malaysian then, 126, clearly deals with the first, the lawyer-client privilege, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at the language carefully, "... for the purpose of his employment as such advocate by or on behalf of his client, or to state the contents or condition of any document with which he has become acquainted in the course and for the purpose of his professional employment", we would say that that extends to communications by third parties to the lawyer acting on behalf of the client.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Even though the rule, I gather, in England and in Australia but to a certain modification is phrased the same way, that they have interpreted two different privileges, one materials collected and the other attorney-client.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It may well be that in the separation of the concepts as a way of dealing with circumstances that may arise for waiver or disclosure, the concepts have been divided. But the essential privilege is that of client-lawyer, and the lawyer being indivisible from the client when he deals with the client as well as third parties. That is the way we look at it and understand it. The Court has been concerned with the Canadian case of Peruta. I must say I read that rather differently and I turn back to the headnote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, when you say "differently", differently from what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Her Honour Judge McDonald, as I understood it, believed that was a set of circumstances that may be more applicable under the American system than under the more limited common law systems.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, I think that Judge Stephen and I, from our questions, may have a difference as to what is said, but this is not the American rule ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was listening to the argument and wondered whether your Honour was believing that Canada came closest to the United States in their system.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, I do not think so. I think that the Prosecutor cannot get the witness statements. It is just the decision, that portion of it, that talks about access on page 19 and page 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In a way, that is a practical problem. If the Defence use a document in court through a witness as a memory refreshing document, which I know your Honour referred to, or any other document, they then cannot keep their privilege when they have disclosed it in evidence in that form. It then would become a statement within the proceedings to be used as a tool, as I understand section 10, sub-section 1 and sub-section 2, of the Act in Canada.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except that the Defence did not use the witness statements to refresh. The Crown wanted them before the Defence began. The trial Judge said "yes", Appeals said "no" and then there is discussion. We have all read it and we can talk about it. So there was no using of the witness statement for refreshment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It seems to have been a peculiar case where everything that could have gone wrong did go wrong ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That was my comment too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- and the heat in the courtroom must have been extreme, but there we are.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That did bring it closer to home, to the United States, you know. I thought as I read it I was back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, we are dealing I think with Quebec here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I did not say any more.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, we have a Judge from Quebec.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But there we are.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, anyway, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, those were the observations I wanted to make on our position which I hope the Court found helpful. If I can deal with any other questions?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, if I may. You gave us Cross & Tapper, 8th edition. Reading it on page 474 it says, last full paragraph, right before "Confidentiality and Waiver": "If a third party is consulted by a legal adviser for the purposes of litigation, perhaps as a potential witness, a question may arise as to the extent to which privilege can be claimed in respect of communications to him. Since there is no property in a witness, the third party is compellable. He is then free to testify, subject to the ordinary operation of legal professional privilege, which will not protects documents submitted to him for expert advice, not otherwise protected. It is dubious how far the old privilege in respect of witness statements can survive the modern practice of requiring disclosure in advance of trial." What does all of that mean? We got it last night and some cases are referred to in the footnote, but I have not pulled them, if I can even find them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the Defence consult a handwriting expert and submit documents to him and he retains possession of copies of the documents, the Prosecution know that you are not going to call him as you have not served him as an expert. They may then go to that witness and use the materials that you still left with the expert as against you. I know, I have been there and I have had it. So, it is something that, in those circumstances, because there is no property in the witness and you have not retained the documents, it may well be the case that they can use that material in relation to their case as against you. If you have submitted specimens of signatures and not taken the copies or the originals back with you, the police could, in those circumstances, use that evidence if they came into their possession. So, it is a rather extreme set of circumstances and one where evidence comes the way of the Prosecution, rather than being part of the formal collection of evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is the witness statement yours? If you take a statement from a witness, witness X, could that witness ask for that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He could ask for that statement ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He says, "Give me a copy of my statement".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- and retain possession of it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then what happens if that witness is called by you ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- and the Prosecutor wants to cross-examine on a prior, inconsistent statement -- alleged inconsistent statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As he would be your own witness and that was your statement, it would not be something that was subject to disclosure. You would say, "That is our material and that is subject to legal professional privilege".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If he had the statement and he wished to say, "Judges, you know, I wish to impress upon you that this is not an inconsistent statement; I am willing to give you this statement", that is not something the witness could give us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. I would call legal professional privilege, unless it was in my interests and was a consistent statement, then I would waive my privilege. But that is our right to waive the privilege.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In your materials you say that the privilege relies in 70(A) of our Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that a privilege that only the Defence has or does the Prosecutor have that privilege, in your view of Rule 70(A)?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Both sides have that privilege, but the difference here is that the Prosecution have to disclose statements to support the indictment. The Prosecution have to disclose statements if they want us to meet a case and be able to deal with a case as part of a continuing trial. If I can just make this observation? We have not received full statements from the Prosecution in relation to all these witnesses. Many witnesses were on short proffers, four or seven lines, and some gave evidence for a day or two and we cross-examined blind. There has not been a full statement given to us for every witness, as would be the system under my jurisdiction where you would disclose and have an orderly list of statements with the content as full as possible of what a witness was proposed to say. There are no procedures within our Rules here that make that explicit.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what the Defence had asked. The Prosecutor had asked, I think, in their pretrial motion as well that if you did not have a statement, that you give a proffer of what the witness would say. Then you said that the statements that you had had been taken in Serbian, then translated into Dutch, then into English ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- and they would not really be very helpful because of the interpretation problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But they had asked for a proffer also. Anyway, 70(A) protects both of them, but because of the burden you would say that it does not protect them as to statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is a necessity for them under the Rules to disclose those statements in support of the indictment. We have not had all those actually. There is outstanding correspondence relating to a number of those witnesses in support of the indictment whose statements we were not given.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The reciprocal discovery rule that we have, Rule 67(C), do you read that as requiring the Defence to provide witness statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. Those are products, material, to be used in evidence, data, that kind of thing. We always had that in mind, that triggering that you produce all your photographs, you produce all your other documents that you were going to use as evidence which we see as being the key phrase underpinning that, and it being a trigger mechanism permits disclosure and access for us to the Prosecution data in terms of material, measurements, whatever, and would then impose the same trigger disclosure upon us.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In Canada, this Rule 10, I think, of the Canadian Evidence Act talks about how the statement should be produced and how you should show it to the witness, etc. We do not have a rule like that in our 10 rules of evidence. Do you think that that in any way affects the Defence counsel's right to cross-examine Prosecution witnesses with respect to prior statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think that is a very much a technical procedural matter, how we go about it in the courtroom. When I put previous statements, Mr. Wladimiroff, Miss de Bertodano did the same, we always put that statement before the witness to give them an opportunity to look at it. Just as a matter of observation here, a large number of those statements were not disclosed to us by the Prosecution, but we obtained by access to the German file and the German proceedings. Therefore, they arose in our hands from the proceedings in Germany where statements had been supplied for the Prosecution authorities there, and we used them within these proceedings for the purposes of inconsistency.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If the Chamber were listening to a witness and perhaps a member of the Chamber were to consider that, one of us or all of us had a question about the witness's veracity and it became apparent that there was a prior statement, you do not believe that the Trial Chamber would have the inherent authority under either 54 or 97 -- I always get 97 and 98 confused, I think it is 98, the power to produce, request product -- 98, do you think that we would then have the power to say to the lawyers: "Look, we have a question about this and we understand there is a prior statement. We would like to have a look at it, not the entire statement but only that portion that deals with the witness's testimony"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This I believe is phrased for the purpose of producing additional evidence in relation to the proceedings themselves. If the Trial Chamber thought that it was necessary for a doctor to be called by the Defence because we were making assertions of a medical nature, you could order us to back it up with medical opinion. That is why it is connected with your power to summons witnesses and order their attendance. The phrase "additional evidence", in our submission, is far too limited to include that specific document of great interest to the Defence, and ordinarily covered by privilege being the witness statements or proofs of evidence that we have taken.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I had a question on the South African or at least the portion of the law we were submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If your Honour could give me the annex, which particular annex it is?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I cannot even find the section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Annex C from the International Encyclopaedia of Laws.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, page 164. Of course, this deals with the Prosecution or the Prosecutor, but they refer to a witness statement privilege. It says: "Written statements obtained from the police for possible witnesses are privileged until after the final conclusion of the trial. This is known as witness statement privilege. The privilege belongs to the Prosecutor and he may waive it. In certain circumstances the Prosecutor must abandon the privilege, for example, where the written statement is used to refresh the memory of the Prosecution witness in the witness box. The Prosecutor must also hand the written statement over to the Defence if there is a serious discrepancy between the written statement of the Prosecution witness and his oral testimony." Then 92(K) is cited in the footnote also which I have not looked at, but it appears that there is something called statement privilege and it appears just from looking at this that that is not something that anyone would get. But if there is a serious discrepancy between the written statement and the Prosecution witness there may be a requirement that it is handed over to the Defence. I was wondering why this sentence is in here if it is not automatically always handed over to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In fact this is long entrenched. We now have very formal discovery rules as a result of miscarriages of justices involving certain cases in England. In the good old days even before I started practise and when I just started practise there was a great deal of playing cards close to the chest and what you were entitled to get and what you -- although we had a formal system of statements, whether you would actually disclose other material where a witness had said something entirely inconsistent in the old days was open to doubt. That was gradually opened up and improved, so that there was much more improved Prosecution disclosure. There was a rule of conduct that if the advocate, the barrister, conducting the case was aware of a previous inconsistent statement that you would then disclose that as a Prosecutor to the Defence, so that you had done your duty. Whether you got to see everything in the old days was another matter and one probably was not given everything anyway. Again that was applying privilege, even to the State which is a very rare concept.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, because in 484 it says "statements obtained by the Defence from prospective Defence witnesses are also privileged."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have whatever this is, six pages, and this is the first time I have read anything about South African law. In any case, it seems to me that both are privileged but then there is something known as this witness statement privilege. Then under (C) which discusses the witness statement privilege it is provided that the Prosecutor must hand the written statement over to the Defence if there is a serious discrepancy between the written statement of the Prosecution witness and his oral testimony. There is no mention anywhere of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It does not say, well, this does not apply to the Defence. I was just asking you. I will check for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It did not apply to the Defence and never has under any system.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How was that? Under what rule is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again it is this principle of who bears the case, who has to present the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Paragraph 481 does not deal with the burden of proof and who has the burden. That perhaps is pretrial. What 481 seems to be talking about is at trial if it appears there is a discrepancy, then it has to be produced. Then in 484 it says that the Defence also has this privilege and I see nothing in here to say that this obligation to produce if there is a discrepancy shown applies to the Prosecutor only, because it is entitled "Witness Statement Privilege" but may be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can advise your Honour it does, and that has been the underpinning of all theory developed from England for 100 years. It has been the underpinning of the system.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So then you would agree with Mr. Wladimiroff, I suppose, that Rule 26.2 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure violate the right to be free from self-incrimination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And it also violates the materials collected or litigation privilege, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is interesting that none of the European States who are signatories to the European Convention on Human Rights have undertaken such a system, although it has been in force in America for many years. The nearest we have got to it is a recent Act within Great Britain involving disclosure by the Defence of the issues in the case, not the statements. The Court may remember the arguments that ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- we had and Judge Vohrah was interested in the matter and aware of these recent developments. But it is not the witness statement, it is not privileged material. It is merely the issues in the case, whether you are running self-defence, intoxication or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I recall you said there was a move towards this more open discovery. If our Rules, though, provide for reciprocal discovery and if our Rules for reciprocal discovery, that is 67(C), include statements, would not that put our whole discussion of this issue in a different frame?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is interesting in that it is a trigger discovery that event (A) causes event (B). We have never been in that position within this case. We have not triggered discovery under those rules. So that even if they would apply and we were in that position in this case, it has not happened. We have not arrived at that stage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand, but even in the United States in the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure there is an obligation on the part of the Defence to trigger this reciprocal discovery. In other words, the Defence has to ask for more than what they would normally get. Then there is a triggering of reciprocal discovery, almost verbatim as our Rules in 67(C). What I am saying is, if that is privileged, if that is privileged, then there is no way for the Rules to require its production even if the duty is only triggered by your asking for information. For example, if 67(C), the reciprocal discovery, were to read, "If you dare to ask for anything under 66(B), then you have to provide communications between your client and yourself", that certainly would not be proper, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. We have always been conscious of the trigger rule, and no witnesses in cross-examination by us were asked to disclose extra statements or anything like that. One does not know the boundaries, but you do not want to trigger something and put yourself in a bad position. So we have conducted this case very carefully in that regard. Any material that we obtained came from the Prosecution or from our own resources. We deliberately sought not to pull the trigger just in case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So if in fact the privilege that the Rules recognise is in 97, the privilege that the Rules recognise is the lawyer-client privilege, in bold type right in the Rules, then certainly it was not the intention, it should not have been the intention, to require that privileged information be produced by 67(C), should it? If it requires statements to be produced, then at least if you assume that the Judges knew what they were doing when they drafted the Rules, then it does not apply to a privilege protected under 97?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is specifically taking out whatever material there would be within 67(C).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is memoranda, reports and any other evidence upon which ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at this logically, we could not use internal communication as between the client and ourselves. It would be inadmissible material and it would not be material that would fall within 67(C). So it is outside anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is why Justice White says in his concurring opinion in Nobles that this kind of rule, this work product rule, is not privileged; it is merely a restriction on discovery, because it is not the kind of thing that you would offer. It is not evidence anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that is clear under the Rules as we have, as your Honour points out, Rule 97.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But you say the privilege is in 70(A). OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the status of 70(A) and what it refers to documents, our statements that we have taken, we would say, would fall within that status of reports, memoranda or internal documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I have one question. It has been said on behalf of the Prosecution that there is waiver of privilege involved in the giving of evidence, and that the giving of evidence by a witness waives the privilege that attaches, in my view anyway, to the witness statement. What do you say as to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The two are totally unconnected, in our submission. It is the document that is the subject of the privilege. The witness gives evidence and in giving evidence offers himself for cross-examination. If we were so foolish enough, and I only use this in a general sense, to say, "Have you made a statement to us entirely consistent with what you are telling the Court now", I have done it, I have put it in. But you do not hear, I hope, advocates asking that kind of question. That would be a waiver of privilege on exactly the same lines as the client saying, "Oh, the solicitor told me not to answer any questions to the police", very dangerous if you are introducing questions and getting that information out because you have partially waived privilege. Of course there is this concept as well of partial waiver. It does not go to full waiver, this partial waiver of privilege. It is interesting how all the jurisdictions apply that theory of partialness, rather than blanket waiver once you have gone so far down a particular course of conduct, how important they view the client-lawyer relationship for the efficacy of their business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have anything in reply, rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Yes, very briefly. I just wish to clear up one matter, at least in relation to what documents we have discovered. We have given all the documents that are required to be given under the Rules in relation to supporting material and so forth. Any proffers that were given or proofs of evidence that were given relate to witnesses where there was no statement. We deny there is any matter outstanding where we have any obligation to disclose. Your Honours, the issue of whether the word "evidence" mentioned in Rule 67(C) included statements was raised. Certainly, if the use of the word "evidence" there does not includes statements, then the obligations of the Prosecutor under Rule 68 is vastly reduced in terms of his obligation to disclose, because large amounts of statements have been disclosed in consequence of Rule 68. It would seem that we have interpreted our obligations much more widely than we thought we had to do. In addition to that, your Honours, under Rule 47 there is a reference there also to evidence to provide reasonable grounds, 47(A). It would seem that in a similar vein if evidence does not include statements, then no obligation arises there either. In our submission, your Honour, to apply an interpretation that evidence relates only to something that is given once the witness enters the witness box, is a very narrow interpretation indeed. Your Honours, in our submission, that is simply not the case because there are numerous provisions that one could point which make reference to things which constitute evidence and they are much wider than simply the witness entering the witness box and giving oral testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The great pity is that we cannot blame an absent draftsman for any defects in these Rules!

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not prepared to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Which Judges usually do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In some of the materials that were submitted, however, there is reference to statements being evidence under certain circumstances, that is, they are used for impeachment purposes but if it can be demonstrated -- well, let us see, I cannot find the Rule but I thought that I read that there were certain circumstances where the statement itself could then be introduced, so it then would become evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, an example of that may be where it is used to prove an inconsistency against a witness, the document which may otherwise not have been evidence or could be described not as evidence would so become. So it is simply too narrow to refer to evidence as being only that which is admitted as evidence before the Chamber and limited only to that. In my submission, the use of the term "evidence" has a broader interpretation and must be given a broader interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I was referring to 1140.8 of the Criminal Law of South Australia where it says: "A prior inconsistent statement proved under Section 29 is not evidence of the truth of the contents of the document but only relates to the credit of the witness." Then it cites cases. "However, the contents of such document may be proved as evidence of its truth under Section 34(C), 45(A) or 45(B) or by any other permissible means. Where a witness who is a party admits making the prior inconsistent statement, that statement becomes evidence of the facts contained in it by virtue of that admission. Where the witness is not a party the contents of the document only become evidence of its truth where he admits them in such a way which its contents become part of his evidence." Anyway, very technical issues of evidence, but it appears that under certain circumstances the statement could be evidence. We are supporting to that rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is our submission. It may or it may not be depending on the circumstances, but it is certainly too narrow simply to say that it only applies once the witness gives evidence. Another matter, your Honours, is that essentially our submission is this, that the full ambit of this whole issue of privilege is catered for in the Rules. It is catered for in Rule 70(A) and it is catered for in Rule 97. They are Rules to which we submit your Honours should return if looking for an interpretation of what is to apply in these circumstances. We urge your Honours that in so doing your Honours apply the principle as is enunciated in paragraph 89(B) in the question of interpretation. At no stage am I saying, in my submission, that the law of the United States should be given preference to any other jurisdiction. All I am saying is that in terms of the most progressive piece of legislation that appears to exist or the most advance system in terms of how the law has developed is that, and we would urge your Honours applying Rule 89(B) ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am one of three Judges. Do you want to pick something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I emphasise again, your Honour, that I am not promoting this system because of that. I am merely promoting it because it is the best formulation of the principle and the most advance formulation of the principle. So, if your Honours are to interpret the provisions, interpret the Rules which are specifically provided here and provide the full ambit, in our submission, of the privilege available in applying Rule 89(B), then this is the best indicia your Honours can go to in terms of formulating a principle to apply in the course of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is just one matter. I know Mr. Niemann is resorting I think now to flattery of the Court in relation to his argument.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think he is flattering the wrong person because he is not looking at a group of American Judges. He is looking at a group of three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Flattery and charm perhaps. Rule 47 is nothing to do with this. This concerns the state of mind of the Prosecutor, that he in his own mind is satisfied there is sufficient evidence because he has researched the case. The operative word in 67(C) is "as" evidence that it is going to be produced in the course of the proceedings and become evidence in the case. The witness statement is not evidence in the case if we do not choose to use it. The Court knows that underpinning all this within these Rules is the obligation to consider the general principles of international law, and this is where I say Mr. Niemann is using flattery because it seems the United States system that he is advancing is actually out of line with all the other systems internationally. It is on a limb, perhaps for particular reasons relating to their jurisdiction and the conduct of cases, but there is underneath all this the obligation on the Court to determine these issues consonant not with national principles or any particular nationality, but principles of general international law. That is what we say we have been working under in relation to this particular matter and the judgment of 7th May.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is just that if you have indicated that there is a move towards wider open discovery, and it is moving along in England but it is moving, then to the extent that 26.2 reflects an opening up of discovery, not discovery but an opening up of material for both sides in the form of allowing for the use of witness statements and the tendering of witness statements once they have testified, then it might be progressive. The Rule in 1978, maybe it was ahead of its time and maybe other countries are moving along slowly, but you are correct, we do not apply the rules of national systems. We will be looking at our Rules, I suppose, to see what there is in our Rules that apply to the positions of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We limited ours under our reform saying that it could go no further without breaching those principles, which was when all these matters were discussed under the Royal Commission that I know Judge Vohrah knows about, and that was as far as the progression was able to go.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 10 minutes and then return with the final ruling on this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (The court adjourned for a short time).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: R U L I N G.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: On September 19th 1996 the Trial Chamber ruled that the prior statement of Witness W was not privileged and was subject to disclosure to the Prosecutor for impeachment purposes. The Trial Chamber has reconsidered that ruling in the light of the written submissions and oral arguments of counsel. By a vote of two to one, with the Presiding Judge dissenting, the Trial Chamber reverses that ruling and finds that such statements are privileged and not subject to the disclosure of the Prosecutor. A decision shall be issued in due course. So we will continue with Witness W tomorrow in closed session. Very good, 10 o'clock. We are adjourned until that time. (The court adjourned until the following day).

procedural_notes.text: (The Court adjourned for a short time)
(The Court adjourned for a short time)
